core.definition: A family, group or organization torn by internal conflict so that it cannot stand united. From Jesus' saying that a divided house cannot stand.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable of divided, which ends in an unstressed id sound. Many learners say 'dih-VIE-ded' with a flat ending; the final syllable is clearly 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes disunity that threatens the group's survival or effectiveness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for political parties, families, sports teams, churches and companies with factions. The phrase has a formal, somewhat weighty tone because of Abraham Lincoln's famous 1858 speech, so it works best in serious talk or writing. A typical reply is 'Yeah, that's the problem with that office right now.'

distinctions.note: A family feud is a long, often personal quarrel; a house divided emphasizes that the group as a whole cannot hold together.
Infighting describes the conflict itself; a house divided describes the resulting state of the group.
Split is a neutral, everyday word for a division; a house divided carries a stronger sense of danger to the whole.

collocations: a house divided over the issue
the party is a house divided

examples.everyday: The whole family is a house divided since Dad and Uncle Ray stopped speaking.
examples.professional: Our leadership team is a house divided, and the product roadmap keeps stalling because of it.
examples.analytical: Lincoln's use of the phrase turns a saying about demonic power in the Gospels into a claim about the moral unity of the nation.

nuance.analogy: Like a building whose load-bearing walls pull in opposite directions until the structure gives way.
nuance.etymology: From Mark 3:25 and its parallels in Matthew and Luke; popularized in American politics by Abraham Lincoln in 1858.
common_mistakes: Taking it literally as a physical house with rooms separated.
Writing 'divided house' as a fixed phrase; the idiom keeps 'a house divided' with 'house' first.
nuance.biblical_note: In Mark 3:24-25, Jesus answers the charge that he casts out demons by Beelzebul by saying that a kingdom, city or house divided against itself cannot stand. Matthew 12:25-26 and Luke 11:17-18 record the same saying, with Matthew adding the city and Luke the kingdom. The Greek word for house is oikia and the verb for divided is merizo. The passages show that Satan's kingdom would collapse if it fought against itself, so Jesus' exorcisms show the power of God at work.

core.definition: A title or name used by several Philistine or Canaanite kings, most notably the king of Gerar in Genesis, and also a son of Gideon who made himself king of Shechem.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable after the initial vowel, BIM. The second and third syllables are weak, and the final 'ek' rhymes with 'check'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name, used mainly in Bible study and sermons, and sometimes in discussions of Gideon's family or Genesis. Americans would not use it as a general word, although the name is recognized as a biblical title for kings.

examples.everyday: At Bible study, we talked about Abimelech, the king who was warned in a dream not to touch Sarah.
examples.professional: In the commentary I'm reviewing, the author compares Abimelech of Gerar with Abimelech of Shechem to show two different uses of the name.
examples.analytical: The title Abimelech in Genesis 20 and Genesis 26 suggests a royal office rather than a single personal name, which raises questions about the historical identity of the king.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Avimelekh', meaning 'my father is king'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the king of Gerar with the son of Gideon, who had a very different story.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Abimelech (Hebrew Avimelekh, 'my father is king') is a royal title or name in the Old Testament. Genesis 20:2-18 tells how the king of Gerar took Sarah, Abraham's wife, and was warned by God in a dream. Genesis 26:1-11 describes a later Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in connection with Isaac. Judges 9:50-54 describes a son of Gideon who killed his brothers, made himself king of Shechem, and was killed when a woman dropped a millstone on his head.

senses.definition: A shrub or tree of the tribe Acacieae.
The thickened or dried juice of several species in Acacieae, in particular Vachellia nilotica (syn. Acacia nilotica, Egyptian acacia).
A false acacia; robinia tree (Robinia pseudoacacia).
Gum arabic; gum acacia.
Any of several related trees, such as a locust tree.
A light to moderate greenish yellow with a hint of red.acacia:
A roll or bag, filled with dust, borne by Byzantine emperors, as a memento of mortality. It is represented on medals.

core.definition: A tree or shrub with feathery leaves and clusters of small yellow or white flowers, native to warm and dry regions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -KAY-, and pronounce the 'ci' as 'sh,' as in 'shuh.' Do not say 'uh-KAY-see-uh.' The last syllable is a reduced 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain botanical term, though it can be pleasant in gardens and florist talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter 'acacia' in gardens, florists' shops, and wood products, and in stores selling cutting boards or furniture. In the American South and Southwest people might also say 'mimosa' for the pink-flowered relative. 'Wattle' is the usual term in Australia, so Americans would not use it.

distinctions.note: 'Mimosa' names a related genus, often with pink puffy flowers and sensitive leaves, and Americans sometimes use it casually for acacia-like trees.
'Wattle' is the common term for acacia in Australia, while Americans normally say 'acacia.'
'Thorn' refers to a sharp growth on a plant; many acacias have thorns, but the word is a general plant part, not a tree type.

examples.everyday: The acacia in our backyard blooms in early spring and the whole yard smells sweet.
examples.professional: The landscape team wants acacia for the courtyard because it tolerates drought well.
examples.analytical: In Exodus the ark is made of acacia wood, so the tree carries cultic meaning as well as botanical identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a desert plant that holds on through drought and still blooms when rain comes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek akakia, from akē 'a point, thorn.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (AH-kah-sha) instead of the second.
Pronouncing the 'ci' as 'see' rather than 'sh.'
nuance.biblical_note: Acacia is the usual translation of the Hebrew word shittah (plural shittim), a desert tree used in the construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings. Exodus 25:10 says the ark is to be made of acacia wood, and Isaiah 41:19 lists the acacia among trees God will plant in the desert. The tree's connection to dry land makes it a sign of God's provision in barren places.

acacia.etymology: From Latin *acacia*, from Ancient Greek *ἀκακία* (“shittah tree”), either from Proto-Indo-European **h₂eḱ-* (“sharp”) (compare *ἀκή* (“point”)) or more likely a word.

senses.definition: A function that retrieves a value, usually without changing any data.
Someone or something that accesses.

core.definition: A method that reads or changes the value of a stored property in a software object, often called a getter or setter.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SES, the same syllable as in the verb access. The final -or is reduced to an r-colored er, not a full or sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in programming.
nuance.usage_note: Programmers use accessor in documentation, code reviews and design discussions, especially in object-oriented languages such as Java and C#. In casual conversation, Americans often say 'getter' or 'setter' instead, and accessor is the general term that covers both.

distinctions.note: A getter is a read-only accessor, a casual name for the method that retrieves a value; accessor is the general term that includes getters and setters.
A mutator is a method that changes a value, while an accessor is the broader term that can mean either reading or writing.

examples.everyday: Our two engineers argued at lunch about whether the accessor should check for null values first.
examples.professional: Add a validation check to the accessor so bad values never reach the database.
examples.analytical: Encapsulation depends on accessors: callers can read a property's value without being able to alter its internal representation directly.

nuance.analogy: Like a front-desk clerk who gives you information from the files but does not let you rewrite them.
nuance.etymology: From access plus the agent suffix -or, from access ultimately from Latin accessus 'approach'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with accessory, which is a completely different word meaning an extra item.
Stressing the last syllable instead of SES.

senses.definition: A high point: the highest point of any range, the most developed stage of any process, or the culmination of any field or historical period.
A paragon: a person or thing representing such a high point.
Sexual orgasm.
Synonym of crisis, the decisive moment in the course of an illness.
(rare) Full bloom or reproductive maturity.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: The highest point of something, or the stage where a person, group, or process is at its very best or most developed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a short, weak 'ee' sound, not a long 'ay'. Don't pronounce it as 'ak-ME'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a peak of quality or achievement, but it sounds elevated, so it works best in writing or a deliberate, formal speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use acme in casual conversation, where they would say peak, top, or best. You will mostly see it in journalism, literary writing, or a playful, slightly grand comment like 'This pie is the acme of desserts.' The word also has a vulgar slang sense referring to orgasm, which is not used in ordinary talk, so avoid it in polite company.

distinctions.note: Peak is the everyday word for a high point of anything. Acme sounds more formal and is often used for the best possible level of skill or quality.
Pinnacle suggests a high point reached after a long climb, often in a career or achievement. Acme is more abstract and sounds more literary.

examples.everyday: This barbecue sauce is the acme of flavor, honestly, you have to try it.
examples.professional: Our team reached the acme of efficiency once the new deployment pipeline went live.
examples.analytical: For Aquinas, the acme of human happiness lies in the contemplation of God rather than in worldly goods.

nuance.analogy: Acme is like the top step of a ladder: you can't climb higher, so you have reached the highest point.
nuance.etymology: From Greek akmē, meaning 'point' or 'highest point'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'ak-ME' with stress on the second syllable.
Using acme for an ordinary good result; it implies an exceptional peak, so 'the acme of quality' is strong praise.

core.definition: A man's name in 1 Chronicles 8:3, listed among the descendants of Benjamin in a genealogy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, as in the month name Adar. Keep the r clear at the end, since Americans pronounce it rhotically.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name found only in biblical genealogies.
nuance.usage_note: Addar is used almost only in Bible study and genealogy discussion, not in everyday American speech. Because it looks like Adar, the month, you should specify 'the man Addar' or 'in 1 Chronicles' to avoid confusion.

distinctions.note: Adar is the twelfth month of the Jewish calendar, while Addar is a personal name in a Benjamite genealogy.

examples.everyday: I found Addar in the genealogy list, but it took me a while to see why he was there.
examples.professional: In the genealogy handout, I'll note Addar among the Benjamite names so students don't confuse him with the month Adar.
examples.analytical: The inclusion of Addar in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 shows the Chronicler's interest in preserving family lines.

common_mistakes: Confusing Addar, the personal name, with Adar, the month.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the last.
nuance.biblical_note: Addar is a personal name in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8:3. The name has no narrative role, and its meaning is uncertain. It is a reminder that the genealogies of Chronicles record many minor names to show tribal descent.

senses.definition: One who advises.
Ellipsis of class adviser.

core.definition: A person who gives expert advice or guidance to someone, often as a professional job or an official role.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VY, which rhymes with 'my.' The 'ad' is unstressed and the final '-er' is an r-colored, reduced vowel. The 's' in the middle sounds like a 'z.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It implies someone trusted with guidance, though the level of formality depends on the setting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans spell this word 'adviser' most often in business and government, while 'advisor' is also widely accepted, especially in universities and by some publications. Use 'adviser' for a financial adviser, academic adviser or campaign adviser. In casual speech, people often say 'advisor' or just name the job, such as 'my financial person.'

distinctions.note: A consultant is usually hired on a project basis for a specific problem, while an adviser may give ongoing guidance over a longer period.
'Advice' is the noun for the guidance itself, and 'adviser' is the person who gives it.

examples.everyday: My financial adviser told me to put more money into my retirement account this year.
examples.professional: As the project's technical adviser, I review the model architecture before each release.
examples.analytical: Plato's dialogues often portray Socrates as an adviser who questions rulers until they discover the limits of their own knowledge.

nuance.analogy: An adviser is like a GPS for a decision: it does not drive the car, but it helps you find the route.
nuance.etymology: From Old French aviser, to consider, from Latin advisare, to look at or consider, from ad- plus visare, to look at.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable as 'AD-vi-zer'; the stress is on the second syllable, VY.
Using 'advise' as a noun; in American English 'advice' is the noun and 'advise' is the verb.

senses.definition: Living or occurring only in the presence of oxygen e.g. aerobic bacteria.
senses.example: The bacteria require an aerobic environment to grow.

senses.definition: Of exercise, performed while maintaining a sufficient supply of oxygen to meet bodily energy needs.
Of or relating to aerobics.
senses.example: She does aerobic exercise three times a week.

core.definition: Relating to exercise that uses oxygen to fuel the body, such as running or cycling, or to organisms that need oxygen to live.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the second syllable, OH, not the first. The first syllable is a quick 'air' sound. Non-native speakers often say AIR-oh-bik, which sounds wrong to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Positive in fitness and health contexts, since it suggests good cardiovascular health. Neutral in biology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use aerobic in health, fitness, and biology. In gyms people often say cardio instead of aerobic exercise, though aerobic is also common. Aerobics is the noun for group exercise classes, so 'I go to aerobics' is natural but 'I do aerobic' alone sounds incomplete.

distinctions.note: Anaerobic means without oxygen, such as short, intense exercise like sprinting. Aerobic is its opposite, using oxygen for sustained effort.
Cardio is an informal gym term for exercise that works the heart. Aerobic is the more precise scientific term.

examples.everyday: I try to get thirty minutes of aerobic exercise, like brisk walking, most days.
examples.professional: The wellness program's sessions focus on aerobic fitness for staff who sit at desks all day.
examples.analytical: Aerobic respiration yields far more ATP per glucose molecule than anaerobic pathways do.

nuance.analogy: Like a steady engine that burns fuel efficiently with plenty of air.
nuance.etymology: From Greek aēr, meaning air, and bios, meaning life.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AIR-oh-bik instead of air-OH-bik.
Using aerobic to mean any active activity; it specifically refers to oxygen-based exercise.

aerobic.etymology: From French *aérobie*, coined in 1863 by Louis Pasteur, from Ancient Greek *ἀήρ* (“air”) + *βίος* (“life”) + *-ic*.

senses.definition: The act of aggravating, or making worse; used of evils, natural or moral; the act of increasing in severity or heinousness; something additional to a crime or wrong and enhancing its guilt or injurious consequences.
Exaggerated representation.
An extrinsic circumstance or accident which increases the guilt of a crime or the misery of a calamity.
A feeling of being provoked by irritation and annoyance; the feeling of being riled up or increasingly irritated.

core.definition: Irritation or frustration caused by a hassle or an annoying situation; also, the act of making a problem worse.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on VAY, and the first two syllables are light, with 'ag' having a secondary stress. The final syllable is a weak 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a frustrating or annoying experience, though in legal contexts it is a neutral term for an aggravating circumstance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a lot of aggravation' or 'more aggravation than it's worth' for everyday hassles, such as bureaucracy, traffic, or repairs. It is common in speech and informal writing. In legal writing it refers to factors that make a crime more serious.

distinctions.note: 'Hassle' is a casual word for a practical nuisance, while 'aggravation' includes the emotional irritation that comes with it.
'Frustration' is the feeling of being blocked from a goal, while 'aggravation' is the irritation caused by a specific annoying situation.
'Annoyance' is usually mild and brief, while 'aggravation' often refers to a longer, more exhausting problem.

examples.everyday: Getting a new license at the DMV is a lot of aggravation, so I planned to go early in the morning.
examples.professional: Fixing the broken pipeline caused a lot of aggravation for the team, but we did ship the release on time.
examples.analytical: Legal aggravation refers to facts that increase the moral or legal seriousness of an offense, such as the use of a weapon.

nuance.analogy: Like a pebble in your shoe that keeps rubbing with every step.
nuance.etymology: From aggravate, from Latin aggravare 'to make heavier', plus the noun suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'agravation' with only one g.
Confusing the noun 'aggravation' with the adjective 'aggravating' when describing a situation.

core.definition: Name of two kings: Ahaziah of Israel, son of Ahab, and Ahaziah of Judah, who ruled only one year before dying.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZY, the third syllable, with a long I like 'eye'. The final syllable is a reduced 'uh' sound, not a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a proper name, used in discussions of the Bible and the kings of Israel and Judah.
nuance.usage_note: As with other biblical names, Americans use this one in church, Bible study, and classes on Scripture. Because two kings share the name, people often say 'Ahaziah of Israel' or 'Ahaziah of Judah' to be clear. Pronounce it the same way in every setting.

distinctions.note: Ahaz is a king of Judah in the eighth century BCE, a different person with a shorter and different name.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading about Ahaziah, who got hurt after falling from an upper room.
examples.professional: When I teach 1 and 2 Kings, I always separate the two kings named Ahaziah so students don't mix them up.
examples.analytical: The narrator of 2 Kings 1 uses Ahaziah's inquiry of Baal-zebub to show that he has turned away from the God of Israel.

nuance.analogy: Like two people in one office who share a first name, you have to add the country to tell them apart.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Ahazyah, meaning roughly 'Yahweh has grasped', combining the name Ahaz with the divine element 'yah'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as a full 'ah' sound instead of a reduced 'uh'.
Stressing the first syllable and saying AY-huh-zy-uh.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew 'Ahazyah' (אֲחַזְיָה), meaning roughly 'Yahweh has grasped', containing the divine name Yah. Key passages: 2 Kings 1:2-17 tells how the king of Israel, injured in a fall, sent messengers to Baal-zebub of Ekron and was rebuked by Elijah; 2 Kings 9:27-28 reports the death of the king of Judah at the hands of Jehu; 2 Chronicles 22:7-9 explains that his downfall came through his visit to Joram, the king of Israel.

senses.definition: Prior to a deadline.
senses.example: Buses are running ahead of schedule, but trains an hour late.

core.definition: Earlier than the planned time for finishing a task, event or project.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HED in ahead and on SKEJ in schedule. Of reduces to uhv, and schedule begins with a hard sk sound, not sh.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals good management and progress, though it can add pressure on a team if used to demand faster work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this constantly in project updates, emails and planning talk, for example 'We shipped the release ahead of schedule.' In standard American English it is usually said without 'the'. A natural reply is 'Nice, that's great news.'

distinctions.note: Early means before a set or expected time in general, while ahead of schedule refers specifically to a planned timeline for a project or task.
Ahead of time is more general and everyday, often used for personal plans, whereas ahead of schedule is typical in business and project management.

examples.everyday: Good news, the contractor finished the kitchen ahead of schedule, so we can move in next weekend.
examples.professional: The design team delivered the prototype ahead of schedule, which gives QA an extra week to test it.
examples.analytical: Judged against its original baseline, the project finished ahead of schedule, though that baseline may have been set too conservatively.

nuance.analogy: Like a train that pulls into the station before the timetable says it should.
nuance.etymology: Ahead comes from a- plus head; schedule comes from Latin schedula, meaning a small slip of paper.
common_mistakes: Saying 'ahead of the schedule', which sounds less natural; the usual form is 'ahead of schedule'.
Using 'before schedule', which is not standard American English.

conversation.text: Good news: we're two days ahead of schedule.
The team finished testing ahead of schedule.
If we stay ahead of schedule, we can add the extra feature.

core.definition: King of Judah from about 642 to 640 BC, son of Manasseh, who was assassinated by his own servants after a reign of about two years.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AY, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say it as AY-mun rather than ah-MON.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and biblical name with no positive or negative charge in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this name in Bible reading, Sunday school or church history, not in ordinary conversation. Do not confuse it with the Egyptian god Amun, which comes up in museum and Egyptology settings.

distinctions.note: Amun is the standard spelling for the Egyptian god, while Amon in the Bible names a king of Judah; context shows which one is meant.

examples.everyday: Did you know King Amon was killed by his own servants after only two years on the throne?
examples.professional: The timeline slide shows Amon ruling only two years before the palace conspiracy, so we should label that gap clearly.
examples.analytical: The Deuteronomistic History presents Amon as a king who did evil like his father Manasseh, which sets up the reforms of his son Josiah.

nuance.etymology: Hebrew personal name 'Amon; its meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing King Amon with the prophet Amos or with the Egyptian god Amun.
Stressing the second syllable and saying ah-MON instead of AY-mun.
nuance.biblical_note: Amon's reign is told in 2 Kings 21:19-26 and 2 Chronicles 33:20-25. Both passages say he did evil as his father Manasseh had done, and that his own servants killed him in his palace. 2 Chronicles 33:23 adds that Amon did not humble himself before the LORD as Manasseh had, and the people of the land then made his son Josiah king. Hebrew: 'Amon (אָמוֹן), a personal name.

senses.definition: A figure of speech in which a word or phrase used at the end of a clause or expression is repeated near the beginning of the next clause or expression.

core.definition: A figure of speech in which the last word or phrase of one clause is repeated at the beginning of the next clause.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PLOH, with a light secondary stress on AN. The middle syllables are reduced to schwas, and the final -sis is a short 'sis', not 'seez'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is usually seen as an effective, memorable device in speech and writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet anadiplosis in English composition, rhetoric, or poetry classes. In everyday talk, people use the device without naming it, such as repeating a key word to emphasize a point. If you need to name it in a meeting, it is safe, but most colleagues will simply say you used a repetition for effect.

distinctions.note: Anaphora repeats the same word at the beginning of successive clauses, while anadiplosis links clauses by repeating the end of one at the start of the next.
Epistrophe repeats words at the end of successive clauses, while anadiplosis moves the repeated word from the end of one clause to the start of the next.

examples.everyday: She said, I'm tired of waiting, waiting for a call that never comes, and that made everyone at the table go quiet.
examples.professional: Our slide says 'data quality matters, quality drives trust', an anadiplosis that makes the point stick with executives.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters often chain clauses through anadiplosis, ending one clause with the word that opens the next and binding the argument together.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay baton passed from one runner to the next, the same word carries the meaning across the handoff.
nuance.etymology: From Greek anadiplōsis, 'a doubling back', from ana- 'again' plus diploun 'to double'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with anaphora, which repeats the start of successive clauses.
Calling any repeated word anadiplosis, when the repetition must link the end of one clause to the beginning of the next.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in AN-uh-duh-PLOH-sis, which weakens the key stress on PLOH.

anadiplosis.etymology: Latin *anadiplōsis*, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek *ἀναδίπλωσις*.

senses.definition: Having analogy, the status of an analogue; corresponding to something else; bearing some resemblance or similar proportion (often followed by "to".)
Functionally similar, but arising through convergent evolution rather than being homologous.

core.definition: Similar to something else in an important way, so that the comparison helps explain it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NAL, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak uh, and the -ous ending reduces to 'us'. Don't say uh-NAL-oh-gus with a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and objective.
nuance.usage_note: Common in science, law and business writing. Americans usually say similar to or comparable to in speech. Analogous to is precise and fits formal writing, and it is almost always followed by 'to'. Avoid it as a stand-in for like in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Similar is general and everyday; analogous suggests a structured correspondence, such as a parallel between two systems.
Homologous means sharing a common evolutionary origin in biology; analogous means similar in function but with different origins.

examples.everyday: Learning a stick shift is somewhat analogous to riding a bike, but it's harder.
examples.professional: The second outage was analogous to the one in March, so the same root cause is likely.
examples.analytical: Legal reasoning is analogous to scientific inference, since both extend known cases to new ones.

nuance.analogy: Like two maps of different cities that share the same grid pattern.
nuance.etymology: From Greek analogos, 'proportionate', from ana- 'according to' and logos 'ratio'.
common_mistakes: Writing analogous with instead of analogous to, the standard construction.
Confusing analogous (an adjective) with analog (a noun meaning counterpart).

analogous.etymology: From Latin *analogus*, from Ancient Greek *ᾰ̓νᾰ́λογος*; Its English equivalent is *analogue* + *ous*.

senses.definition: Acronym of analysis of covariance.

core.definition: Statistical method combining ANOVA and regression to compare group means while statistically adjusting for continuous covariates.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say ANCOVA as one word, not as the letters A-N-C-O-V-A. Stress falls on the first syllable, and the last syllable is a reduced uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone and is used only in statistics and research contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists, statisticians, and researchers in fields like psychology, medicine, and public health use ANCOVA in conversation and reports. It is usually introduced with a full phrase the first time, such as 'analysis of covariance,' and then shortened to ANCOVA.

distinctions.note: ANOVA compares group means using only categorical factors, while ANCOVA also adjusts for continuous variables called covariates.
MANCOVA extends ANCOVA to several dependent variables at once, so it is used when outcomes are measured together.

collocations: adjusted for covariates in an ANCOVA

examples.everyday: My sister is a biostatistician, and she said she had to run an ANCOVA to make the two groups comparable.
examples.professional: Let's run an ANCOVA with baseline score as the covariate before we report the treatment effect.
examples.analytical: An ANCOVA isolates the treatment effect by holding the continuous pretest scores constant across groups.

nuance.analogy: ANCOVA is like comparing two runners' finish times after adjusting for how far each one started behind the line.
nuance.etymology: Acronym of analysis of covariance; the method was developed by R. A. Fisher in the 1930s.
common_mistakes: Saying the letters A-N-C-O-V-A instead of the word AN-koh-vuh.
Using ANCOVA for categorical covariates only, when ANCOVA specifically requires continuous covariates.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or suffering from anemia.
Weak; listless; lacking power, vigor, vitality, or colorfulness.
A person who has anemia.

core.definition: Having anemia, or lacking energy, strength, or color in a way that seems weak or pale.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NEE, the second syllable. The final syllable is a short i sound, like in 'kick' rather than 'keek.'

nuance.connotation: Often negative when used figuratively to describe a weak performance, a dull result, or a lifeless design. Medically, it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anemic medically to describe patients, and figuratively in business or media to say that a result is weak, such as 'anemic sales growth.' Saying someone is anemic in a casual conversation can sound clinical or rude if they do not have the condition.

distinctions.note: Pale describes the color of skin or a surface, while anemic can describe medical weakness or, figuratively, a weak and lifeless quality.
Weak is general and common, while anemic suggests a lack of vigor or vitality, often in a figurative sense about results or performance.

examples.everyday: I felt anemic after the flu, so I slept most of the weekend and drank a lot of juice.
examples.professional: Our quarterly numbers look anemic, so we need a clearer plan before the board meeting.
examples.analytical: The critique calls the policy's anemic response a symptom of institutional inertia rather than of budget limits.

nuance.analogy: An anemic result is like a phone battery that never gets above twenty percent: it still works, but it lacks the power to do much.
nuance.etymology: Formed from anemia, from Greek anaimia, meaning without blood.
common_mistakes: Using anemic for a person who is just tired, which can sound unkind.
Spelling it anaemic, which is British.

senses.definition: Ancient times; faraway history; former ages.
senses.example: Cicero was an eloquent orator of antiquity.

senses.definition: The people of ancient times.
The historical period preceding the Middle Ages (c. 500-1500), primarily relating to European history.
A relic or monument of ancient times, such as a coin, a statue, etc. an ancient institution.
The state of being ancient or of ancient lineage.

core.definition: Ancient times, especially the distant past before the Middle Ages, or an old object or work from that period.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -TIK-, and the final -ity is unstressed, sounding like tee. The middle vowel is a quick schwa, so say an-TIK-wuh-tee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests age, tradition, and importance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use antiquity mainly when talking about ancient history, Greece and Rome, or old artifacts in museums. In everyday speech they might just say 'ancient times' or 'really old.' Saying 'We found an object of antiquity' sounds formal, so use it for emphasis or in writing.

distinctions.note: Ancient times is the everyday phrase, while antiquity is more formal and often refers to the classical world of Greece and Rome.
Antique is an object that is valuable and old, while antiquity is the period itself or a very old thing from it.

examples.everyday: That old wooden chair is pure antiquity; my grandmother has had it forever.
examples.professional: The archive contains manuscripts from antiquity, so we will need a historian to review them before publication.
examples.analytical: Medieval thinkers often read antiquity through Aristotle, treating classical texts as the foundation of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Antiquity is like the bottom layer of a deep canyon: the older rock is the foundation that everything later sits on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin antiquitas, from antiquus (old, ancient), with the suffix -tas forming a state or quality.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in AN-tik-wi-tee.
Using antiquity to mean an old object only; it usually refers to the ancient period as a whole.

antiquity.etymology: From Middle English *antiquyte*, *antiquite*, *antiquytee*, a borrowing from Old French *antiquité*, *antiquitet*, from Latin *antiquitas*, from *antiquus*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to knowledge of God obtained through negation rather than positive assertions.
That passively defines a thing by describing what is not characteristic of it.

core.definition: Describing knowledge of God reached by saying what God is not, rather than by making positive statements about God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAT. The t in the stressed syllable is a hard t, not a flap, because it comes after the stress. The first syllable has secondary stress with the vowel of 'cat.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent; it signals humility before divine mystery.
nuance.usage_note: Used in theology, philosophy, and spirituality, especially about Eastern Orthodoxy and mystics like Gregory of Nyssa and Pseudo-Dionysius. Typical phrases are 'apophatic theology' and 'apophatic tradition.' It would sound odd outside religious or philosophical talk.

distinctions.note: Cataphatic theology affirms positive attributes of God; apophatic denies them.
'Negative theology' is a synonym, but 'apophatic' is the more technical and common scholarly term.
Mystical refers to direct experience; apophatic refers to a method of speech and thought, though the two often overlap.

examples.everyday: My friend from the Orthodox church explained that their approach to prayer is very apophatic, more silence than words.
examples.professional: This week's lecture will introduce the apophatic tradition and its place in patristic theology.
examples.analytical: An apophatic theology insists that every human concept falls short of God, yet it does not abandon speech about God altogether.

nuance.analogy: Like describing an unseen object by its outline: you say 'not this, not that' until only mystery remains.
nuance.etymology: From Greek apophatikos, from apophasis, 'denial.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (AP-uh-fat-ik).
Thinking it means 'atheistic' or simply 'negative' in the everyday sense.

senses.definition: Asking whether a doctor can take you as a regular patient.

core.definition: Asking whether a doctor, dentist, or clinic is willing to take on new people as regular patients.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEP in accepting and on PAY in patients. Phrases link smoothly, so 'are you' sounds like 'ahr-yoo', and 'accepting' is not stressed on its first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It is a routine question when looking for a new doctor.
nuance.usage_note: This is the standard phrase Americans use when calling a doctor's office or dentist. Many offices are full, so staff may say 'We're not taking new patients right now' or 'Let me check.' Americans often follow up with 'Do you take my insurance?' because coverage matters a great deal. To begin the call, you can say 'Hi, I'm looking for a new primary care doctor.'

distinctions.note: Taking and accepting mean the same thing here; both are natural American phrases.
This asks about insurance coverage, which is a separate and very common follow-up question.
Clients is used for lawyers, accountants, or consultants; patients is the word for medical care.

examples.everyday: Hi, I just moved here. Are you accepting new patients for checkups?
examples.professional: Our office manager asked me to call; are you accepting new patients for the occupational health clinic?
examples.analytical: The question 'Are you accepting new patients?' reveals how scarce primary care access has become in many US communities.

nuance.analogy: Like asking whether a restaurant has any open tables before you walk in.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Are you accepting new patient?' with the singular; the natural form is the plural patients.
Stressing accepting on the first syllable, as in AK-sep-ting, which sounds unclear to Americans.

conversation.text: Hi, are you accepting new patients? I just moved here.
Are you accepting new patients, or is there a waiting list?
Are you accepting new patients this year? My kids need a dentist.

senses.definition: An upstart or newcomer; nouveau riche; parvenu; an ambitious, brash or arrogant person who has yet to integrate with his or her new social group.

core.definition: A person who pushes ambitiously to gain wealth or social status, especially someone not yet accepted by the group they want to join.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the last syllable, so say 'ar-ee-VEEST' with a strong final 'veest'. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the ending as 'vist'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies someone who is pushy, opportunistic or insincere in climbing socially.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in casual talk; it appears in essays, political commentary, novels, and sharp observations about social climbing. It is a judgment, so calling someone an arriviste to their face would be insulting. You are more likely to hear 'social climber' in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Social climber is the everyday American equivalent and is more casual; arriviste sounds more literary and formal.
A newcomer is simply someone new to a place or group, with no negative judgment; an arriviste is ambitious and pushy about entering.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is such a social climber; she's always name-dropping at the block party.
examples.professional: Some senior managers see him as a corporate arriviste, always angling for the next promotion.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays its protagonist as a ruthless arriviste whose ambition exposes the hollowness of the old aristocracy.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who pushes to the front of a wedding photo, eager to be seen with the family who has not yet invited them.
nuance.etymology: From French arriviste, from arriver, 'to arrive', from Old French ariver, from Latin ad ripam, 'to the shore'.
common_mistakes: Using arriviste for any newcomer, when the word specifically implies pushy social ambition.
Stressing the first syllable as 'AR-ih-vist' instead of the final syllable.

core.definition: A king of Judah (about 910-870 BC) who removed idols, reformed worship and relied on God to defeat a huge Ethiopian army.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AY, and the final -a is a weak uh sound. Do not add an extra syllable or pronounce it ah-sah as in Spanish.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear Asa mostly in Bible study or as a first name. When discussing the king, people usually say King Asa of Judah to make the reference clear.

examples.everyday: Our Sunday school class is reading about King Asa this week, and the teacher says he was a good king.
examples.professional: In my commentary notes I compared the account of King Asa in Kings with the fuller version in Chronicles.
examples.analytical: The accounts of Asa in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles emphasize different aspects of his reign, and the Chronicler reads his story as a lesson about trusting God.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Asa; its root meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it ah-sah as in Spanish.
Confusing Asa with Asaph, another name in the Psalms and Chronicles.
Adding an extra syllable at the end.
nuance.biblical_note: Asa was the third king of Judah after Solomon's kingdom divided. 1 Kings 15:9-24 describes his removal of idols and his reign, including an alliance with Ben-hadad of Aram. 2 Chronicles 14:9-15 records his victory over the Ethiopian army through prayer, and 2 Chronicles 16:7-10 describes the prophet Hanani rebuking him for trusting Aram rather than God. Matthew 1:7-8 includes Asa in the genealogy of Jesus. The Hebrew name is Asa, meaning uncertain.

senses.definition: To separate or reduce into atoms.
To make into a fine spray.
senses.example: What every tinkerer with a homegrown Otto engine needed at this time was a better carburetor to atomize the fuel.

senses.definition: To fragment; to break into small pieces or concepts.
senses.example: What every tinkerer with a homegrown database management system needed at this time was a better database model to atomize the data.

senses.definition: To deprive of community and political capital.
To bomb with nuclear weapons.

core.definition: To break something into very small particles or pieces, or to spray a liquid into a fine mist.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, AT. The final -ize is pronounced like 'eyes', not like 'iz' in 'his', so it is one clear diphthong sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical and everyday uses. Used figuratively, it suggests that something valuable has been broken apart and destroyed, which is negative.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American life, you meet this word most often in its noun form 'atomizer', the spray bottle for perfume. The verb is common in science, engineering, and cooking, such as 'atomize the fuel', and in social criticism, where 'atomize society' means to make people isolated from one another. In casual speech, 'spray' or 'break up' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Pulverize means to crush into powder with force, while atomize means to break into very fine droplets or particles, often by spraying.
Fragment means to break into pieces, often accidentally, while atomize implies a fine, uniform breakup, usually by design.
Vaporize means to turn into gas or vapor by heating, while atomize keeps the material as tiny liquid or solid particles.

examples.everyday: This perfume bottle's atomizer is clogged, so can you spray it under hot water to clear it?
examples.professional: The nozzle is designed to atomize the coolant into a fine mist so it evaporates faster across the heat sink.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that market logic atomizes social life, leaving individuals with few shared commitments.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass dropped on tile: it breaks into shards, but atomizing makes the pieces so fine they become a mist.
nuance.etymology: Formed from atom plus the verb-forming suffix -ize; atom comes from Greek atomos, 'uncuttable'.
common_mistakes: Confusing atomize with atomic, which is an adjective (atomic energy, atomic weight).
Stressing the second syllable (uh-MAIZ) instead of the first (AT-uh-maiz).

senses.definition: To arrive at (a certain age or time, condition or state, etc.); to reach.
To gain (a desired result or other objective) through effort; to accomplish, to achieve.
senses.example: To attain such a high level of proficiency requires hours of practice each day.

senses.definition: To reach (someone) after being behind them.
To find out (information, knowledge, etc.); to ascertain, to get at.
Often followed by to.
To arrive at a certain condition or state, etc.
To extend or reach from one position to another; to stretch.
To find out information, knowledge, etc.
To gain a desired result or other objective through effort.
Of a person: to live to a certain age or time.
Of a thing: to befall, to happen to someone.
Synonym of attainment.
An act of arriving at or reaching; an act of obtaining by effort.
That which is obtained by effort.

core.definition: To reach or achieve a goal, status, or level after sustained effort over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable TAYN, which rhymes with 'rain' and 'brain'. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, so keep it weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies that a goal was reached through effort, perseverance, or long preparation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'attain' mainly in formal writing, speeches, and career or academic contexts, such as 'attain a degree'. In casual speech they say 'reach', 'get to', or 'achieve'. The noun 'attainment' is common in education, as in 'educational attainment'.

distinctions.note: Achieve is the common everyday word for accomplishing something, while attain is more formal and often suggests reaching a state or level.
Reach is plain and general, and it can be physical, while attain implies effort and a goal worth working for.
Obtain means to get something, often by request or acquisition, and it does not necessarily imply sustained effort.

examples.everyday: She finally attained the goal she had been chasing for years when she ran her first marathon.
examples.professional: The team attained its quarterly target two weeks early, so we need to revisit next quarter's goals.
examples.analytical: Aristotle held that eudaimonia is attained through sustained virtuous activity, not through pleasure or wealth.

nuance.analogy: Like reaching the top of a staircase after climbing every step, one by one.
nuance.etymology: From Old French ataindre, from Latin attingere, 'to reach, touch', from ad- + tangere 'to touch'.
common_mistakes: Confusing attain with obtain, attend, or attempt, which have different meanings and often different prepositions.
Using 'attain to' in modern English where 'attain' alone is more natural.

attain.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *atteinen*, *atteynen* (“to achieve, attain; to be adequate or sufficient; to affect; to come or get to, reach; to corrupt, taint; to overcome, overpower; to overtake; to succeed; to tamper with; to bring to justice,…

senses.definition: Grinding down or wearing away by friction.
A gradual reduction in number.
A gradual, natural reduction in membership or personnel, as through injury, incapacitation, retirement, resignation, or death.
The loss of participants during an experiment.
The loss of a first or second language or a portion of that language.
Imperfect contrition or remorse.
The wearing of teeth due to their grinding.
To grind or wear down through friction.
senses.example: attritioned teeth; attritioned rock

senses.definition: To reduce the number of (jobs or workers) by not hiring new employees to fill positions that become vacant (often with out).
To undergo a reduction in number.
senses.example: The cohort of one hundred students had attritioned to sixty by the end of secondary school.

core.definition: The gradual loss of people or things over time, such as employees leaving without being replaced or participants dropping out of a study.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRI, the middle syllable, and the ti is pronounced 'sh', not 'tee'. The final -tion sounds like 'shun', so say uh-TRISH-un, not uh-TRIT-ee-un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes loss over time and often implies a problem, such as high turnover or dropout.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, attrition mainly refers to employees leaving without being replaced, and it is common in HR and management meetings. In statistics and research it means participants dropping out of a study. In casual talk Americans say 'turnover' or 'people leaving', so attrition can sound too formal in conversation.

distinctions.note: Turnover covers all departures, voluntary or not; attrition specifically describes a gradual loss, often through people who leave and are not replaced.
A dropout is one person who quits a program or study; attrition is the overall rate of loss across a whole group over time.

examples.everyday: A lot of people on my old team left last year, so there's been a lot of attrition.
examples.professional: Our attrition rate is six percent, so we need to plan hiring for the next two quarters.
examples.analytical: Survey attrition is often nonrandom: participants who drop out tend to be the least satisfied, which biases the results.

nuance.analogy: Attrition is like a sandcastle eroding with each wave, losing a little sand at a time until it is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin attritio, a rubbing against, from atterere, to wear away.
common_mistakes: Using attrition for a single sudden departure; it describes a gradual, cumulative loss over time.
Pronouncing the tt as a hard double t or saying 'at-tri-tion' with the stress in the wrong place; say uh-TRISH-un.

attrition.etymology: from Middle English *attricion*, *attricioun*, from Middle French *attricion*, *attrition* and its etymon, Latin *attrītiō* (“a rubbing against”), from the verb *attrītus*, past participle of *atterō* (“to wear”), from *ad-* + *terō*.

senses.definition: A personal condition or state of self-reliance; independence.
(A policy of) national economic self-sufficiency, aimed at ending reliance on foreign imports to sustain a domestic economy.
A self-sufficient country or region which is not dependent on international trade to function economically.

core.definition: A state of economic self-sufficiency in which a country produces what it needs and avoids depending on foreign trade.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable: AW-tahr-kee. The first vowel is the aw of law, and the middle syllable has an r-colored ah. Do not say OH-tar-kee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics; it can sound negative when criticizing isolation and positive when praising self-reliance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use autarky mainly in economics, political science and history. In everyday conversation they say 'economic self-sufficiency' or 'self-reliance.' The word often appears in debates about closed economies, such as North Korea or Nazi Germany's pre-war economic policy.

distinctions.note: Autarchy means absolute rule by one person; autarky means economic self-sufficiency. The words look alike but are not synonyms.
Autonomy means independence or self-governance in general; autarky specifically means economic self-sufficiency.

examples.everyday: My uncle keeps talking about autarky, which he thinks means we should make everything ourselves.
examples.professional: The trade policy group warned that a push for autarky would raise costs for our manufacturing clients.
examples.analytical: Autarky is the economic condition in which a state can satisfy its needs without trade, a goal that usually reduces efficiency.

nuance.analogy: Autarky is like a household that grows all its own food, makes its own clothes and never goes to the store.
nuance.etymology: From Greek autarkeia, self-sufficiency, from autos 'self' and arkein 'to suffice'.
common_mistakes: Confusing autarky with autarchy, which means absolute rule by one person.
Putting the stress on the second syllable; say AW-tahr-kee.

autarky.etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek *αὐτᾰ́ρκειᾰ* (“independence, self-sufficiency, autarky; satisfaction with one’s resources, contentment”) + *-y*.

senses.definition: To withdraw from something one has agreed to do.
senses.example: She backed out of organizing the fund-raising.

senses.definition: To convince (someone) to withdraw from a challenge.
To reverse (a vehicle) from a confined space.
senses.example: He backed out of the garage.

senses.definition: To bet on someone losing.
senses.example: See also: sell short

senses.definition: To undo (a change).
senses.example: I had to back out the changes made to the computer when it became apparent that they had stopped it working properly.

senses.definition: To exit a mode or function.
senses.example: I chose that menu option by accident, so I pressed Escape to back out.

senses.definition: To draw from behind the back (a knife etc.) (as also bare back).

core.definition: To withdraw from a plan, deal or commitment that you had already agreed to, usually at the last minute.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OUT, which carries the diphthong /aʊ/, similar to 'ow'. Keep back short and crisp, and do not stretch the vowel into 'bayk'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests unreliability or letting people down, especially when it happens late.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use back out in everyday plans, for example 'Sorry, I have to back out of dinner tonight.' It sounds more casual than withdraw and more personal than cancel. In business, Americans may say pull out or withdraw for a more formal tone. A natural reply is 'No worries, let's reschedule.'

distinctions.note: Cancel is neutral and can be done by either side, while back out implies you had committed and are now withdrawing.
Drop out means leaving a course, team or competition, while back out suggests reneging on a promise or agreement.

collocations: back out at the last minute

examples.everyday: Sorry, I have to back out of the movie tonight because my kid is sick.
examples.professional: The vendor backed out of the contract two days before signing, so we're reopening the procurement process.
examples.analytical: A rational agent may back out of a promise when new information changes the expected value of keeping it.

nuance.analogy: Like taking your name off a guest list after the invitations have gone out.
nuance.etymology: Back comes from Old English bæc; out comes from Old English ūt; the phrasal verb is native English.
common_mistakes: Saying back out the plan instead of back out of the plan; the preposition of is needed.
Forgetting that back out can also mean reversing a car, so context determines the meaning.

conversation.text: He backed out of the deal at the last minute.
You promised to help me move, so don't back out now.
Watch for kids when you back out of the driveway.
I'll back the car out so you can get the bikes.

senses.definition: To refill a hole with the material dug out of it.
To refill an excavation unit to restore the former ground surface and/or to preserve the unit and make it recognizable as having been excavated.
To provide reserve support.
To replenish or restock due to attrition or loss.
senses.example: The company backfilled Joe's position after he was terminated.

senses.definition: To enter an online game that's already in progress, replacing a player who left early.
The material that has been used to refill an excavation.
Reserve support personnel.
That which backfills; a replacement.
Material in a story set earlier in the past, providing history or context for the current action.

core.definition: In data work, to fill in missing or historical records by reprocessing past data, such as recomputing earlier dates.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, BACK. The second syllable has a short i as in sit, not a long ee, and the final l is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In data teams it is an everyday operational word, though a non-technical listener may hear it as replacing people.
nuance.usage_note: In data science, Americans say 'backfill the table' or 'backfill last month's data' when a pipeline has gaps or needs history added. Outside tech, it is common in construction and landscaping, as in 'backfill the trench.' If you are not sure which sense someone means, ask whether they mean data or physical work.

distinctions.note: Refill means filling something again. Backfill specifically means filling gaps behind something or in past records.
Backfill fills gaps in history that were missing. Reprocess reruns a job on data that already exists.
Fill in is a general phrase. Backfill implies going back in time or filling space behind something.

examples.everyday: My landscaper is going to backfill the trench next to the driveway tomorrow.
examples.professional: We need to backfill three months of event data so the dashboard matches what finance reported.
examples.analytical: Backfilling historical records raises questions about whether past predictions used information that was actually available at the time.

nuance.analogy: Like patching the holes in a wall after the old pictures come down, so the record looks complete.
nuance.etymology: From back plus fill. It first meant refilling an excavation, and the data sense came later by extension.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean refilling a glass or container. In data work it means filling gaps in history.
Confusing it with backlog, which is unfinished work waiting in a queue.
Pronouncing the vowel in fill as a long ee.

senses.definition: With the back of the hand.
Involving a backward flip of the hand.
Insincere, sarcastic, ironic, or self-contradictory.
Indirect.
Backwards, turned around.
Inclining to the left.
Retrospective, occurring after the fact rather than in advance.
Self-serving, corrupt, slipshod, or neglectful.
In a backhanded manner.

core.definition: Insincere or indirect in a way that seems like praise but is really an insult or sly criticism, as in a backhanded compliment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on BACK, the first syllable. The ending -ed is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like id, not a separate ay sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a remark that hides criticism behind a compliment or a polite surface.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use backhanded mostly for compliments or remarks that hide an insult, as in 'That's kind of a backhanded compliment.' Calling someone's remark backhanded can sound harsh if they meant it nicely, so use it when you are sure. A natural reply to a backhanded compliment is a wry 'Thanks, I think.'

distinctions.note: Sarcasm says the opposite of what you mean in a mocking way. A backhanded remark is a compliment that conceals criticism.
Irony usually signals contrast or wit. Backhanded specifically implies a veiled jab.
A backhand is a stroke in sports. The figurative backhanded describes remarks, not strokes.

examples.everyday: She said my new haircut was brave, which was a bit of a backhanded compliment.
examples.professional: His feedback was backhanded: he praised the speed but questioned the quality of the code.
examples.analytical: A backhanded compliment works by letting the praise carry a hidden judgment that the speaker can later deny.

nuance.analogy: Like a gift wrapped in a nice box that turns out to hold something unpleasant.
nuance.etymology: From the back of the hand used to strike someone, so a backhanded blow comes from an unexpected or sly direction.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean simply indirect. It implies a hidden insult, not just indirectness.
Pronouncing the ending -ed as a separate syllable, as in BAK-han-ded.
Using it for a sincere but awkwardly worded compliment.

senses.definition: To confuse or perplex (someone) completely; to bewilder, to confound, to puzzle.
senses.example: I am baffled by the contradictions and omissions in the instructions.

senses.definition: To dampen, muffle, restrain, or otherwise control (a fluid, or waves traveling through a fluid such as light or sound).
To deceive or hoodwink (someone); to gull.
Followed by away or out: to deprive of (something) through cheating or manipulation; also (followed by out of), to deprive of something by cheating or manipulating (someone).
To expend effort or struggle in vain.
senses.example: The ship, baffling with the winds, moved not an inch.

senses.definition: To publicly disgrace (someone); specifically, a recreant knight.
To treat (someone) with contempt; to disgrace; also, to speak of (someone or something) in contemptuous terms; to speak ill of, to vilify.
Of weather or wind: to hinder or prevent (a ship or its crew) from advancing.

A device used to dampen, muffle, restrain, or otherwise control the movement of a fluid, or waves traveling through a fluid such as light or sound; specifically, a surface positioned inside an open area to inhibit direct motion from one place to another without preventing motion altogether.
senses.example: Tanker trucks use baffles to keep the liquids inside from sloshing around.

senses.definition: A device to prevent the spreading of sound or light.
senses.example: sound baffle

senses.definition: A barrier designed to obstruct and confuse enemies, rendering them vulnerable.

core.definition: To confuse someone so completely that they cannot understand or explain something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to a weak 'l' sound, so do not add a full vowel and say 'BAF-uh-ul'. Remember the double f in the spelling.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes a feeling of being stuck or defeated by something hard to understand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'baffle' in everyday conversation and at work, often in phrases like 'That baffles me.' It is a bit stronger than 'confuse' and suggests that your attempts to understand have failed. A natural reply to someone who says it is 'Yeah, I know, right?' or 'Me too.'

distinctions.note: Confuse is the general, everyday word; baffle implies that the thing has defeated your attempts to understand it.
Puzzle suggests that you might solve the problem with thought, while baffle suggests the problem resists every solution.
Perplex is more formal and suggests a prolonged mental tangle, while baffle is more common in speech.

examples.everyday: Why my car won't start on cold mornings baffles me every single winter.
examples.professional: The accuracy drop after the schema change has baffled the whole team, so we need to rerun the test.
examples.analytical: Many readers are baffled by how Hume, an empiricist, can still defend our belief in causation so confidently.

nuance.analogy: Like a maze with no exit, where every path you try turns your thinking back on itself.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the earliest sense was to thwart, disgrace, or treat with contempt.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with one f, as in 'bafle'.
Using 'baffle of' or 'baffled of'; the common structure is 'baffled by' or 'baffled at'.

baffle.etymology: The origin of the verb is; it is possibly:

senses.definition: An agreement between parties concerning the sale of property; or a contract by which one party binds themself to transfer the right to some property for a consideration, and the other party binds themself to receive the property and pay the consideration.
An agreement or stipulation; mutual pledge.
An item purchased for significantly less than the usual, or recommended, price.
A gainful transaction; an advantageous purchase.
senses.example: to buy (something) at a bargain

senses.definition: The thing stipulated or purchased.
To make a bargain; to make a deal or contract for the exchange of property or services; to negotiate; to haggle.
senses.example: They had to bargain for a few minutes to get a decent price for the rug.

senses.definition: To transfer for a consideration; to barter; to trade.

core.definition: An item bought for much less than its usual or recommended price, or a good deal that offers real value.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to 'gin,' not 'gayn,' so it sounds like the word 'gin' with a quick, weak vowel. The g is clearly pronounced, not silent.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests you got good value, though a bargain that is low quality can feel like a waste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'What a bargain!' or 'That's a bargain' when they buy something cheap. In casual talk, people also say 'It's a steal' for an extremely good price. When talking about a deal between people, 'bargain' still works, as in 'strike a bargain.' A natural reply to 'That's a bargain' is 'Right? I couldn't pass it up.'

distinctions.note: Deal can mean an agreement or a discount, while bargain specifically emphasizes getting good value for a low price.
Steal is more informal and suggests an extraordinarily cheap price, sometimes almost too good to be true.

examples.everyday: That jacket was only twenty dollars, which is a real bargain for something so warm.
examples.professional: The software license renewal is a bargain compared with what we paid last year, so let's sign before the price changes.
examples.analytical: Economists often treat a bargain as a gap between perceived value and price, which means its worth depends on the buyer's own judgment.

nuance.analogy: A bargain is like a fair scale that balances what you pay against what you receive, and tips a little in your favor.
nuance.etymology: From Old French bargaignier, meaning to haggle or dispute over a price.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a bargain price' as if the word needs 'price'; 'a bargain' alone is natural.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'gayn' instead of a short 'gin' sound.

bargain.etymology: From Middle English *bargaynen* (“to bargain, make a pledge for sale”), from Old French *bargaigner* (“to bargain”), from **borganjan* (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Germanic **burgijaną* (“to borrow, lend”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰergʰ-* (“to…

conversation.text: These boots were a bargain at thirty dollars.
My grandma loves hunting for bargains at yard sales.
That couch was a real bargain compared to what we saw downtown.

senses.definition: The property of being barren; the property of not supporting life.

core.definition: The state of being barren, with poor soil, no plant growth, lifeless surroundings, or inability to bear children.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The n of barren carries into the -ness ending, so the sound is one held n followed by a short, unstressed -ess.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting emptiness, failure, or sadness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barrenness mostly in writing or thoughtful speech about landscapes, soil, or a feeling of emptiness. For a person's infertility, they would more likely say infertility. You might describe the barrenness of a desert or the emotional barrenness of an office after layoffs.

distinctions.note: Emptiness means nothing is inside or nobody is present; barrenness adds the sense that nothing can grow or be produced.
Desolation adds a sense of sorrow or loneliness; barrenness is more about lack of life or fertility.

examples.everyday: I still can't get over the barrenness of that dried-up lake; there's no life left in it.
examples.professional: The barrenness of the Q3 pipeline made the forecast look shaky.
examples.analytical: Her memoir turns the barrenness of exile into a meditation on what remains when everything familiar is gone.

nuance.analogy: Barrenness is like an empty garden in winter: the ground is there, but nothing is growing.
nuance.etymology: From barren plus -ness, the English suffix meaning state or condition.
common_mistakes: Spelling it with a double n, as barrenness, when the correct spelling has a single n
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long a, as in bare-ness, instead of the air sound

senses.definition: In AI: A standard set of tasks used to measure and compare models.
A standard by which something is evaluated or measured.
A surveyor's mark made on some stationary object and shown on a map; used as a reference point.
A computer program that is executed to assess the performance of the runtime environment.
To give certain results in a benchmark test.
To use something (e.g. a competitor's product) as a standard to improve one's own thing.
To measure the performance or quality of (an item) relative to another similar item in an impartial scientific manner.

core.definition: A standard or reference point, often a test or set of tasks, used to measure and compare performance or quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BENCH, and keep the second syllable short and reduced. The final 'k' should be clearly pronounced, and the r in 'mark' is fully rhotic in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a factual, objective word, though in business it can imply a goal to aim for.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use benchmark constantly at work, in tech, finance, and sports, and in everyday talk about comparing prices or results. Saying 'That's our benchmark' in a meeting is natural and not stiff. In everyday conversation, you might hear 'Use last year's sales as a benchmark' or 'Let's set a benchmark for ourselves.'

distinctions.note: A standard is a general norm or expectation; a benchmark is a specific measurable reference point used for comparison.
A metric is a quantity that you measure; a benchmark is a reference value or test set you measure against.
A baseline is the starting point before a change; a benchmark is a target or comparison point, often from an external standard.

examples.everyday: Our old car gets forty miles per gallon, so I use that as my benchmark when I shop for a new one.
examples.professional: Let's compare our latency numbers against the industry benchmark before we ship the release.
examples.analytical: A benchmark is only as meaningful as the questions it asks, so we should examine what the test really measures.

nuance.analogy: Like the pencil lines a carpenter marks on a wall to check whether a shelf is level.
nuance.etymology: From the surveyor's 'bench mark', a mark cut into a fixed object such as a stone bench, used as a reference height.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ben-CHMARK) instead of the first.
Using 'benchmark' only for tests; in everyday English it also means any standard for comparison.
Forgetting the 'ch' sound and saying 'BEN-mark'.

conversation.text: A benchmark is a fixed dataset and metric that lets researchers compare models.
We benchmarked three embedding models on our own queries.
A high benchmark score doesn't guarantee good performance on our data.
Their customer satisfaction scores are the industry benchmark.

core.definition: A member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes of ancient Israel descended from Jacob's youngest son.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BEN. The last syllable rhymes with "bite," so do not reduce it to "-it" as in "sit."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Use this word mainly in Bible study, history, or religious writing when you need to describe a person from the tribe of Benjamin. In everyday speech, you would normally just say "from the tribe of Benjamin" instead.

distinctions.note: Both are used, but Benjamite is the more common spelling in standard English Bible translations and reference works.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies Bible history told me that Saul was a Benjamite.
examples.professional: In my sermon on the tribes of Israel, I explained that Saul was a Benjamite from a modest family.
examples.analytical: The Benjamite tribe nearly disappeared after the civil war recorded in Judges 20, which shaped how later writers remembered that tribe.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who says they are from a particular county rather than a state, a Benjamite identifies with one specific tribe inside Israel.
nuance.etymology: Formed from Benjamin, the name of the tribe's ancestor, with the English suffix -ite meaning a member of a group.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in "ben-ja-MITE."
Using "Benjamite" as a general term for anyone named Benjamin.
nuance.biblical_note: Benjamites are members of the tribe descended from Benjamin, son of Jacob. Ehud, a judge who delivered Israel from Moab, was a Benjamite (Judges 3:15). Saul, Israel's first king, came from a Benjamite family (1 Samuel 9:1-2). Mordecai, who helped Esther, is also described as a Benjamite (Esther 2:5).

senses.definition: Made or done in a way adjusted to the needs of a specific person or group (e.g. customer, health care patient, do-it-yourselfer), and thus specialized and, in some cases, unique.
Relating to someone who makes custom-made products, especially clothing items.
senses.example: a bespoke tailor

core.definition: Made specifically to a customer's order and measurements, rather than mass-produced; custom-made or tailor-made.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SPOHK, which rhymes with "joke." The first syllable is a short, reduced "bih," and the final "k" is a clear, sharp sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Bespoke is used mostly in British English for tailored suits, shoes and high-end products, and Americans would rarely use it in conversation. The American equivalent is custom-made, tailor-made or made-to-order. You may still see bespoke in luxury advertising or software and consulting writing.

distinctions.note: Custom-made is the everyday American term and is more common in stores and conversation, while bespoke sounds more British or luxurious.
Tailor-made is used for clothes and also for things adjusted to a specific purpose, and it sounds natural in American speech.

examples.everyday: My brother got a suit made just for him, and the tailor said it was completely custom, so I'm calling it a bespoke suit.
examples.professional: Our vendor offered a bespoke analytics dashboard, but we decided a standard tool would meet our needs faster.
examples.analytical: The distinction between bespoke and mass-produced goods raises questions about how value is created in a market that prizes individual craftsmanship.

nuance.analogy: A bespoke suit is like a key cut for one lock; it fits exactly one customer, and no other.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of bespeak, meaning "to order in advance," so bespoke means "ordered in advance."
common_mistakes: Using bespoke as a noun, as in "a bespoke for my dress."
Using it in everyday American speech where custom-made or tailor-made would sound more natural.

core.definition: Town in Judah, south of Jerusalem, meaning 'house of bread'; the birthplace of King David and of Jesus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BETH; the middle syllable is a reduced 'luh', and the last syllable is lighter. Many learners wrongly stress the middle: beth-LEE-hem.

nuance.connotation: Positive and sacred in religious contexts, linked to Christmas and the nativity; neutral as a place name, as in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Bethlehem with stress on the first syllable, and they connect it strongly with Christmas carols such as 'O Little Town of Bethlehem'. In casual talk you can name a trip to 'Bethlehem' in Israel or the Pennsylvania city without explanation. Add 'Pennsylvania' or 'the West Bank' if the listener may not know which one you mean.

distinctions.note: Bethlehem is the town where Jesus was born; Bethel is the place of Jacob's dream. Both names mean 'house of', but they are different places.

examples.everyday: My aunt went to Bethlehem on a church trip last year and brought us olive wood carvings.
examples.professional: The Bethlehem office in Pennsylvania is moving its data team to the main campus next quarter.
examples.analytical: Matthew links Jesus' birth to Bethlehem and presents the town as the fulfillment of Micah's prophecy of a ruler from there.

nuance.analogy: Like a hometown that a whole story is built around, the place where something important began.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew bêt-leḥem, 'house of bread'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the middle syllable, beth-LEE-hem.
Mixing up Bethlehem with Bethel, which is a different place.
nuance.biblical_note: Bethlehem is Hebrew bêt-leḥem, 'house of bread', a town in Judah also called Ephrathah. 1 Samuel 16:1 identifies it as the home of Jesse, David's father. Micah 5:2 prophesies that a ruler will come from Bethlehem Ephrathah. Matthew 2:1-6 reports that Jesus was born in Bethlehem in the days of Herod and cites Micah's prophecy. Luke 2:4-7 tells how Joseph and Mary went to Bethlehem, the city of David, where Jesus was born and laid in a manger.

bethlehem.etymology: Middle English *Bethleem*, from Old French *Bethleem* and Old English *Bethleem*, from Latin *Bēthlehēmum*, from Ancient Greek *Βηθλεέμ*, from Hebrew *בֵּית לֶחֶם*.

senses.definition: Obvious, on show; unashamed; loudly obtrusive or offensive.
senses.example: a blatant breach of good faith in the negotiation

core.definition: Done so openly and obviously that it is clearly wrong, with no effort made to hide it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BLAY. The second syllable is weak, so the ending sounds like tunt, not the ant of an insect.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes wrongdoing or offensiveness that is done shamelessly in plain view.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use blatant in news, workplace complaints and everyday talk about obvious lies, unfairness or cheating: a blatant lie or blatant discrimination. It is stronger than obvious and signals that the person doing it does not care who sees. It is common in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Obvious is neutral and means easy to see; blatant adds a negative sense that something bad is done openly and without shame.
Flagrant emphasizes a shocking violation of rules or norms; blatant emphasizes that the wrongdoing is visible and unashamed.
Overt means openly stated or done and is not necessarily bad; blatant almost always implies something wrong or offensive.

examples.everyday: He cut right in front of us in line, and that was just blatant.
examples.professional: The vendor's blatant disregard for the contract terms is why we're escalating this to legal.
