examples.analytical: The argument is blatantly circular, since it assumes the conclusion it claims to prove.

nuance.analogy: Like a neon sign in a dark room: you can't miss it, and that's the problem.
nuance.etymology: Coined by Edmund Spenser in The Faerie Queene (1590s) for a monstrous Blatant Beast; the origin is probably imitative of noisy bleating.
common_mistakes: Using blatant to mean simply big or clear without the negative sense of wrongdoing.
Confusing blatant with latent, which means hidden or present but not yet visible.

senses.definition: A good thing; a thing to be thankful for or to appreciate duly.
senses.example: Finding the dry cave was a boon to the weary travelers.

senses.definition: That which is asked or granted as a benefit or favor; a gift or benefaction.
A blessing, typically a supernatural power, granted to an ascetic by a god or goddess.
The woody portion of flax, separated from the fiber as refuse matter by retting, braking, and scutching.
Gay; merry; jovial; convivial.

core.definition: Something helpful or welcome that makes life easier or better, a real advantage or blessing.

pronunciation.tip: This word is a single syllable that rhymes with 'moon' and 'soon'. Keep the vowel long and do not add a y sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a welcome benefit, often one that people did not expect or greatly appreciate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boon in writing, speeches and thoughtful conversation. It sounds a little old-fashioned in casual speech, so for everyday talk, say 'a real help' or 'a lifesaver'. You might hear 'a boon to the community' in news articles or public statements.

distinctions.note: Benefit is a general word for advantage. Boon is stronger and more emotional, suggesting something that is a real blessing.
Blessing often has a religious or emotional meaning. Boon is more practical and can describe things like technology or policy.

examples.everyday: The new bike lane has been a real boon for getting around town without a car.
examples.professional: Automating the report generation has been a boon for the whole analytics team.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers have argued that free inquiry is a boon to any society that wants to improve its understanding of truth.

nuance.analogy: Like rain after a long drought, a boon arrives at the right moment and makes everything easier.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse bón, meaning prayer or request, which came to mean a favor granted.
common_mistakes: Confusing boon with boom, which is a loud sound or a rapid growth period.
Using boon as a verb; it is almost always a noun in modern English.

boon.etymology: From Middle English *boon* (“prayer”), from Old Norse *bón* (“prayer, petition”), from Proto-Germanic **bōniz* (“supplication”), influenced by *boon* (“good, favorable”). see there for more.

senses.definition: To remove or alter those parts of a text considered offensive, vulgar, or otherwise unseemly.
senses.example: The bowdlerized version of the novel, while free of vulgarity, was also free of flavor.

core.definition: To remove or change the sexual, vulgar, or offensive parts of a text, film, or speech.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is BOHD, with the 'oh' vowel as in 'go', not 'how'. The middle -er- is a reduced, r-colored vowel, and the ending rhymes with 'prize'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to critical; it implies unwanted editing that weakens the original.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bowdlerize mainly about books, films, song lyrics, or classic texts edited for children or general audiences. It sounds literary, so in everyday speech people more often say censor, clean up, or sanitize. You will hear it in book clubs, news about edited classics, and debates over school reading lists.

distinctions.note: Censor is broader and can mean suppressing whole works; bowdlerize means editing parts of a text to remove offensive material.
Sanitize is common everyday English for making content cleaner or less risky; bowdlerize is more literary and specifically about text.
Abridge means shorten, usually for length; bowdlerize means remove offensive content, though an edition may do both.

examples.everyday: My dad refused to let us watch the bowdlerized version of the movie, so we just read the book.
examples.professional: Brand managers asked us to bowdlerize the copy, so we removed the risky phrases before publishing.
examples.analytical: Some scholars argue that bowdlerizing Shakespeare replaced his frank language with Victorian concern for propriety.

nuance.analogy: To bowdlerize a text is like scrubbing a painting until the parts people dislike disappear.
nuance.etymology: Named after Thomas Bowdler, who published a family edition of Shakespeare in 1807 with objectionable material removed.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as bow-DLER-ize instead of BOHD-luh-ryze.
Using bowdlerize for any removal of content; it applies specifically to offensive or vulgar material in texts.

senses.definition: Having difficulty breathing; gasping.
That makes one hold one's breath (with excitement etc.).
Not breathing; dead or apparently so.
Having no wind; still, calm or airless.
Having a somewhat hysterical tone, using over-emotive language.

core.definition: Out of breath, gasping for air after exertion, or so excited or surprised that you stop breathing normally.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'breath', and the final '-less' is a reduced 'lus'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing physical exertion; positive when describing excitement or awe, as in breathless anticipation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use breathless for running, climbing, or emotional moments. A person might say 'I'm breathless from running for the bus.' In writing, breathless often describes a dramatic or exciting tone. Calling someone breathless in a romantic sense can sound poetic or flirtatious.

distinctions.note: Out of breath is the common everyday phrase, while breathless is a single adjective that can also describe excitement or awe.
Winded is informal and refers mainly to physical exhaustion, while breathless can describe emotion too.

examples.everyday: I got so breathless running up the hill that I had to sit down.
examples.professional: The team was breathless with excitement when the test results finally came in.
examples.analytical: The narrator's breathless prose conveys the suspense of the moment as the characters wait for judgment.

nuance.analogy: Being breathless is like a car running out of fuel; the body cannot take in enough air to keep going.
nuance.etymology: From breath plus the suffix -less, meaning without breath.
common_mistakes: Using breathless to mean 'breathtaking', which describes beauty or scenery; it is closer to 'out of breath'.
Pronouncing the 'th' as a voiced sound as in 'breathe'; in the noun 'breath' it is voiceless.

senses.definition: To strike (a person), originally with something flat or heavy, but now specifically in such a way as to discolor the skin without breaking it; to contuse.
To damage the skin of (fruit or vegetables), in an analogous way.
Of fruit or vegetables, to gain bruises through being handled roughly.
senses.example: Bananas bruise easily.

senses.definition: To become bruised.
senses.example: I bruise easily.

senses.definition: To fight with the fists; to box.
To harm or injure somebody's feelings or self-esteem.
senses.example: Her thoughtless remarks bruised my ego.

senses.definition: To impair (gin) by shaking rather than stirring.
A purplish mark on the skin due to leakage of blood from capillaries under the surface that have been damaged by a blow.
A dark mark on fruit or vegetables caused by a blow to the surface.

core.definition: A discolored mark on the skin caused by a blow, where small blood vessels under the skin have broken.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, rhyming with 'news' or 'choose', with a voiced z at the end. Do not add an extra vowel as in 'BROO-see'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It refers to injury, but it is a common and mild word in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say I got a bruise or I bruise easily when talking about themselves. Informally, people might say a black-and-blue mark, though that is more old-fashioned. For fruit, Americans say bruised bananas or bruised apples, and the word is used in grocery and cooking contexts as well.

distinctions.note: A cut breaks the skin and shows an opening, while a bruise leaves the skin intact but discolored.
A welt is a raised ridge on the skin, often from a whip or insect bite, while a bruise is flat and discolored.
Contusion is the medical term for a bruise, used in clinical notes and insurance forms.

examples.everyday: I bumped into the coffee table and got a huge bruise on my leg.
examples.professional: The insurance form asks for the location and size of any bruise sustained in the accident.
examples.analytical: The poem uses the bruise as a metaphor for memory, showing harm that remains hidden beneath an unbroken surface.

nuance.analogy: A bruise is like a stain under the skin, where the damage is hidden but still visible in color.
nuance.etymology: From Old English brȳsan, meaning to crush.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel sound and saying 'BROO-see'.
Using bruise as a verb in cases where Americans would say hurt or injure, or treating bruise as only a noun.

bruise.etymology: From Middle English *bruisen*, *brusen*, *brosen*, *brisen*, *bresen*, from a merger two words, both ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **bʰrews-* (“to break”):

conversation.text: I have a big bruise on my leg, but I don't remember hitting anything.
The bruise turned purple and then yellow.
I bruised my arm when I bumped into the table.

senses.definition: A telephone conversation; a phone call.
senses.example: I received several phone calls today.

senses.definition: A decision or judgment.
senses.example: That was a good call.

senses.definition: A cry or shout.
senses.example: He heard a call from the other side of the room.

senses.definition: The characteristic cry of a bird or other animal.
senses.example: That sound is the distinctive call of the cuckoo bird.

senses.definition: A beckoning or summoning.
senses.example: I had to yield to the call of the wild.

senses.definition: An instance of calling someone on the telephone.
senses.example: I made a call to Jim, but he didn’t answer.

senses.definition: A short visit, usually for social purposes.
senses.example: I paid a call to a dear friend of mine.

senses.definition: The right to speak at a given time during a debate or other public event; the floor.
senses.example: The Prime Minister has the call.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of call option.
A work shift which requires one to be available when requested, i.e. on call.
The act of jumping to a subprogram, saving the means to return to the original point.
A statement of a particular state, or rule, made in many games such as bridge, craps, jacks, and so on.
senses.example: There was a 20 dollar bet on the table, and my call was 9.

senses.definition: The act of matching a bet made by a player who has previously bet in the same round of betting.
A note blown on the horn to encourage the dogs in a hunt.
A pipe or other instrument to call birds or animals by imitating their note or cry. A game call.
An invitation to take charge of or serve a church as its pastor.
A meeting with a client for paid sex; hookup; job.
Need; necessity.
senses.example: There's no call for that kind of bad language!

senses.definition: A visit by a ship or boat to a port.
senses.example: The ship made a call at Southampton.

senses.definition: The act of calling to the other batsman.
The state of being the batsman whose role it is to call (depends on where the ball goes.)
A whistle or pipe, used by the boatswain and his mate to summon the sailors to duty.
A reference to, or statement of, an object, course, distance, or other matter of description in a survey or grant requiring or calling for a corresponding object, etc. on the land.
A lawyer who was called to the bar (became licensed as a lawyer) in a specified year.
To make a decision as a referee or umpire.
senses.example: The goal was called offside.

senses.definition: To name, identify, or describe.
senses.example: Why don’t we dispense with the formalities? Please call me Al.

senses.definition: To name or refer to.
senses.example: Why don’t we dispense with the formalities? Please call me Al.

senses.definition: Of a person, to have as one's name; of a thing, to have as its name.
senses.example: I’m called John.

senses.definition: To reach out with one's voice.
senses.example: That person is hurt; call for help!

senses.definition: To request, summon, or beckon.
senses.example: That person is hurt; call for help!

senses.definition: To cry or shout.
senses.example: "Supper's ready," called Dad from the kitchen.

senses.definition: To utter in a loud or distinct voice.
senses.example: to call the roll of a military company

senses.definition: To contact by telephone.
senses.example: Why don’t you call me in the morning?

senses.definition: To rouse from sleep; to awaken.
To request that one's band play (a particular tune).
To visit.
senses.example: We could always call on a friend.

senses.definition: To pay a (social) visit (often used with "on", "round", or "at"; used by salespeople with "again" to invite customers to come again).
senses.example: We could always call on a friend.

senses.definition: To stop at a station or port.
senses.example: This train calls at Reading, Slough and London Paddington.

senses.definition: To come to pass; to afflict.
To state, or estimate, approximately or loosely; to characterize without strict regard to fact.
senses.example: They call the distance ten miles.

senses.definition: To claim the existence of some malfeasance; to denounce as.
senses.example: I call bullshit.

senses.definition: To declare, or declare in favor of, a predicted or actual result.
senses.example: The captains call the coin toss.

senses.definition: To declare in advance.
senses.example: The captains call the coin toss.

senses.definition: To predict.
senses.example: He called twelve of the last three recessions.

senses.definition: To formally recognize a death: especially to announce and record the time, place and fact of a person’s death.
To declare (an effort or project) to be a failure.
senses.example: After the third massive failure, John called the whole initiative.

senses.definition: Direct or indirect use of the voice.
senses.example: Every shot must be called.

senses.definition: To equal the same amount that other players are currently betting.
senses.example: I bet $800 and Jane raised to $1600. My options: call (match her $1600 bet), reraise, or fold.

senses.definition: To match the current bet amount, in preparation for a raise in the same turn. (Usually, players are forbidden to announce one's play this way.)
senses.example: I’ll call your 300, and raise to 600!

senses.definition: To state, or invoke a rule, in many games such as bridge, craps, jacks, and so on.
senses.example: My partner called two spades.

senses.definition: To require, demand.
senses.example: He felt called to help the old man.

senses.definition: To cause to be verbally subjected to.
senses.example: The basis for his conclusion was called into doubt

senses.definition: To lay claim to an object or role which is up for grabs.
senses.example: I call the comfy chair!

senses.definition: To announce the early extinction of a debt by prepayment, usually at a premium.
To demand repayment of a loan.
To jump to (another part of a program); to perform some operation, returning to the original point on completion.
senses.example: A recursive function is one that calls itself.

senses.definition: (of a batsman): To shout directions to the other batsman on whether or not they should take a run.
(of a fielder): To shout to other fielders that he intends to take a catch (thus avoiding collisions).
To tell in advance which shot one is attempting.
senses.example: Every shot must be called.

core.definition: A telephone conversation; a time when you speak with someone by phone.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with the vowel of 'caught', which in American English is the same as the vowel of 'cot' for many speakers. Keep the 'l' light and clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is the ordinary, everyday word for a phone conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'give me a call' or 'I'll call you back' all the time. 'Telephone call' sounds formal or written. In speech, 'a call' almost always means a phone call, so 'I got a call from my sister' is natural.

distinctions.note: 'Ring' describes the sound a phone makes, while 'call' describes the conversation; 'I'll ring you' sounds British.
A video call adds a camera; a regular call is audio only, and Americans say 'FaceTime' or 'video call' to specify.

examples.everyday: Give me a call when you get off work, and we'll figure out dinner.
examples.professional: I took a call from the client, so I'm a few minutes late to the stand-up.
examples.analytical: Each call in the transcript was coded by topic, which made the pattern of complaints visible.

nuance.analogy: Like a short meeting that happens over the phone instead of in a room.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ceallian, probably from Old Norse kalla, to shout or summon.
common_mistakes: Saying 'do a call' instead of 'make a call' or 'take a call'.
Using 'ring' for the conversation itself, which sounds British in American speech.

call.etymology: From Middle English *callen*, from Old English *ċeallian* (“to call, shout”) and Old Norse *kalla* (“to call; shout; refer to as; name”); both from Proto-Germanic **kalzōną* (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European **golH-so-* (“voice, cry”),

conversation.text: I'll call you tonight after dinner.
I was on a call with a client all morning.
"Should we get pizza or tacos?" "Your call. I'm fine with either."
What do you call this thing in English?

senses.definition: A person who calumniates (slanders, or makes personal attacks upon, others).

core.definition: A person who spreads false and harmful accusations about someone in order to damage their reputation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LUM. The final syllable is a rhotic 'er' sound, so pronounce it clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It labels someone as a malicious liar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use calumniator mostly in formal writing, commentary, or literary contexts, not in everyday conversation. It is a strong word, so calling someone a calumniator in public can seem heated or self-consciously formal. In normal speech, people say 'liar,' 'slanderer,' or 'the person spreading those rumors.'

distinctions.note: Slanderer is a plain, everyday word for someone who spreads false spoken statements, while calumniator is more formal and literary.
A critic may give fair, honest criticism, while a calumniator deliberately spreads false and damaging charges.

examples.professional: Don't let that calumniator on the forum distract you; the metrics we shared show the real picture.
examples.analytical: The essay portrays the political pamphleteer as a calumniator whose method depended on insinuation rather than evidence.

nuance.analogy: A calumniator is like a rumor mill, grinding out false flour that others bake into bread they then eat.
nuance.etymology: From calumniate plus the agent suffix -or; calumniate comes from Latin calumniari, 'to accuse falsely.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress as KAL-oo-mun-ee-ator.
Using calumniator as a neutral word for any critic instead of someone who spreads falsehoods.

senses.definition: A piece of jewelry, etc. carved in relief.
A single very brief appearance, especially by a prominent celebrity in a movie or song.
senses.example: Famous comic book writer Stan Lee had a cameo in the Spider-Man movie. He was on screen for perhaps ten seconds, but aficionados distinctly remember him.

senses.definition: To appear in a cameo role.

core.definition: A very brief appearance in a movie, TV show, or song, often by a famous person who plays a small role.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAM. The word has three syllables, and the final vowel is an 'oh' sound. Don't use the Italian-style 'kuh-MAY-oh' pronunciation.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually signals a fun surprise, though a cameo can sometimes feel like a publicity stunt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cameo constantly when talking about movies, TV, and music videos, especially when a celebrity shows up for a moment. It is informal but common in both casual talk and entertainment journalism. You might say 'She had a cameo in the finale.' A natural reply is 'Wait, really? I didn't even notice her!'

distinctions.note: A walk-on role is a tiny part, often without lines, usually played by someone not famous, while a cameo features a recognizable person.
A guest appearance is a larger role or set of appearances on a TV show, while a cameo is typically one brief moment.
A supporting role is a substantial part that supports the main story, while a cameo is brief and often used as a surprise.

examples.everyday: Did you catch the celebrity cameo at the end of the show? It was so unexpected.
examples.professional: Marketing wants to book a celebrity cameo for the product launch video so it gets more shares.
examples.analytical: Hitchcock's famous cameos functioned almost as a signature, inviting viewers to look for him as part of the film's self-aware play.

nuance.analogy: A cameo is like a guest knocking on the door for just one scene, then leaving before anyone can ask for an autograph.
nuance.etymology: From Italian cammeo, a carved gem or shell, referring to a small figure set in relief. The film sense extends this image of a small, distinct figure.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'kuh-MAY-oh' in the Italian style; American English usually stresses the first syllable.
Using cameo to mean a major or leading role; it means a short appearance.
Confusing the verb 'to cameo' with the noun; both are used, but the noun is far more common in everyday speech.

cameo.etymology: Borrowed from Italian *cammeo*, from Medieval Latin *camaeus*, of origin.

conversation.text: The director made a quick cameo in the movie.
Did you catch the cameo at the end?
There's a surprise cameo in the last episode.

can-i-get-a-salad-instead-of-fries.phonetic: /kæn aɪ ˌɡɛt ə ˌsæləd ˌɪnˌstɛd ʌv ˈfɹaɪz/

senses.definition: Asking to swap the side dish that comes with your meal; "sub" is the casual verb: "Can I sub a salad for the fries?"

core.definition: A polite way to ask to replace the fries or another side dish that comes with your meal with a salad.

pronunciation.respelling: kun eye get uh SAL-ad in-STED uv FRAYZ
pronunciation.tip: In fast speech, 'Can I' sounds like 'kin eye,' 'get a' sounds like 'git uh,' and 'instead of' sounds like 'in-STED-uv.' Stress SAL in 'salad' and STED in 'instead.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a polite request that servers hear all the time.
nuance.usage_note: This is a standard, friendly request in American restaurants, and it is normal to ask for a substitution at casual places. Some restaurants charge a small upcharge for a salad, so you may hear 'there's a charge for that.' A natural reply is 'Sure, no problem' or 'Yes, we can do that.'

distinctions.note: 'Could I have' is slightly more formal; 'Can I get' is the everyday restaurant phrasing.
'Sub' is a casual verb meaning to substitute, as in 'Can I sub a salad for the fries?'

examples.everyday: Can I get a salad instead of fries? I'm trying to eat lighter this week.
examples.professional: At the client lunch, the vendor's manager asked, Can I get a salad instead of fries, if the kitchen has one?
examples.analytical: A diner who asks, Can I get a salad instead of fries? signals a preference for substitution, which restaurants should price and display clearly.

nuance.analogy: Asking for a salad instead of fries is like swapping one part of a set combo for another, as if you were trading a song on a playlist.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'of' and saying 'instead fries' instead of 'instead of fries.'
Using 'Can I get' at formal banquets, where 'May I have' sounds more appropriate.

conversation.text: The burger sounds great. Can I get a salad instead of fries?
I'm trying to eat lighter. Can I get a salad instead of fries, please?

senses.definition: Something that encourages progress or change.
senses.example: Economic development and integration are working as a catalyst for peace.

senses.definition: An inciting incident that sets the successive conflict into motion.
A catalytic converter.
An object that facilitates the casting of a spell (such as a magic wand).
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.

core.definition: Something that causes or speeds up a process or change, or a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed by it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAT. The middle syllable is reduced to a weak 'uh,' and the final syllable is a short 'list,' so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it usually describes something that helps progress or change, though in chemistry it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'catalyst' in business, politics, and everyday talk about change, like 'the new manager was a catalyst for change.' In chemistry and engineering it has a precise meaning. It is a common word in meetings and presentations, so it is worth mastering.

distinctions.note: A trigger starts something quickly, often suddenly; a catalyst speeds up or enables a change that was already developing.
A driver is a main cause or force behind something; a catalyst is more like the spark that accelerates it.

examples.everyday: Losing my job was the catalyst for me to start my own business.
examples.professional: The new API release was the catalyst for rewriting our entire reporting pipeline.
examples.analytical: For many scholars, the Reformation acted as a catalyst for changes in European education and print culture.

nuance.analogy: Like a match thrown into dry leaves: it does not become part of the fire, but it starts the blaze.
nuance.etymology: From Greek katalysis 'dissolution,' from katalyein 'to dissolve.'
common_mistakes: Using catalyst for something that causes a change in the wrong direction, when a trigger or cause is meant.
Pronouncing the middle syllable clearly as 'ah' instead of a reduced 'uh.'

senses.definition: The investing of money into a third party's lawsuit in which one has no vested interest.

core.definition: A legal doctrine that bars investing in someone else's lawsuit in exchange for a share of any money won.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final syllables are reduced to a weak ur and tee, not a long ee vowel. It is a specialized legal term that most people will never need outside law.

nuance.connotation: Negative in legal contexts, because courts often treat it as improper or against public policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans hear champerty mainly from lawyers, judges, and law students. Some states still apply it, while others have changed the rules for litigation funding. Outside law, people would say third-party litigation funding or a financial stake in a lawsuit.

distinctions.note: Maintenance means supporting someone's lawsuit without a share of the winnings; champerty adds a financial share of the outcome.
Modern third-party litigation funding is often legal and regulated, while champerty is the older doctrine that can void such deals in some states.
Champion means a winner or advocate; the words look similar, but champerty is only a legal term.

examples.everyday: I don't really understand champerty, but my lawyer said our deal with that investor might be illegal.
examples.professional: Before we sign, legal needs to confirm that the funding agreement doesn't violate champerty rules in this state.
examples.analytical: The doctrine of champerty protects the integrity of litigation by preventing outside parties from profiting from disputes in which they have no legitimate stake.

nuance.analogy: Like buying a share of a stranger's lawsuit and then demanding a cut of the award, when the court asks whether you had a real interest in the case.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman champartie, from Old French champart, a share of the harvest owed to a landlord.
common_mistakes: Confusing champerty with champion, which means a winner or advocate
Treating it as a general word for any funded lawsuit; it is a specific legal doctrine

champerty.etymology: From Middle English *champartie*, from Middle French *champart* (“field rent”), probably from Latin *campī* (“fields”) + *pars* (“part”).

senses.definition: In AI: A saved copy of a model's weights at a point during training.

A situation, often represented by a point in time, at which the state of a database system is known to be valid, and to which it can be returned in the event of a crisis by using a combination of backups and logs; the data stored at this event.
senses.example: After the crash, we rolled back the database to the last checkpoint.

senses.definition: A point or place where a check is performed, especially a point along a road or on a frontier where travelers are stopped for inspection.
senses.example: The travelers were stopped at the checkpoint.

senses.definition: A predetermined point in a map, level or scenario that the player may resume from if they die or restart.
senses.example: You can't finish the race if you haven't passed all of the checkpoints on the track.

senses.definition: A biological control mechanism ensuring correct progression through the cell cycle.
To set a checkpoint.

core.definition: A place where people or vehicles are stopped and checked, such as at a border or an airport; in machine learning, a saved copy of a model's state, including its weights, used to resume or restore training.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on CHEK, with a lighter secondary stress on POINT. Do not stress the second syllable, and keep the final /nt/ clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. In everyday English it can mean a security point, so context decides meaning.
nuance.usage_note: ML teams say 'save a checkpoint,' 'load the latest checkpoint,' or 'resume from a checkpoint' in standups and code reviews. Outside tech, Americans usually mean a security line at an airport when they say checkpoint, as in 'TSA checkpoint.' A natural reply in a meeting is 'The one from last Tuesday, before the learning rate change.'

distinctions.note: A snapshot is any saved state, while an ML checkpoint specifically saves model weights and training information so training can resume.
Save file is an informal, general term, while checkpoint is the precise technical term in ML and databases.
In everyday US life, checkpoint usually means a security screening area at an airport, so specify the context when you mean ML.

examples.everyday: Hey, did you save a checkpoint before the GPU node crashed? I don't want to start over.
examples.professional: Let's resume the run from the latest checkpoint so we don't lose the last six hours of training.
examples.analytical: A checkpoint captures weights and optimizer state at a specific step, so reproducing a run also requires saving the data order.

nuance.analogy: Like a save point in a video game: when the run crashes, you restart from there instead of the beginning.
nuance.etymology: From 'check' (to verify) plus 'point,' a place where something is verified; the computing sense is a later extension.
common_mistakes: Treating a checkpoint as just the model file; it is a saved training state at one moment.
Stressing the second syllable as 'chek-POYNT' rather than CHEK-poynt.

conversation.text: We save a checkpoint every thousand steps so a crash doesn't cost us the whole run.
Which checkpoint is in production, the one from step 40k or the final one?
We waited forty minutes at the airport security checkpoint.

senses.definition: An official summons or notice given to a person to appear.
The paper containing such summons or notice.
The act of citing a passage from a text, or from another person, using the exact words of the original text or speech and giving credit to the original by referencing.
An entry in a list of sources from which information was taken, typically following a prescribed bibliographical style; a reference.
An instance of having had one's work cited.
senses.example: She has over 1,000 citations.

senses.definition: The passage or words quoted; a quotation.
A quotation with attached bibliographical details demonstrating the use of a particular lexical item in a dictionary, especially a dictionary on historical principles.
Enumeration; mention.
senses.example: It's a simple citation of facts.

senses.definition: A reference to decided cases, or books of authority, to prove a point in law.
A commendation in recognition of some achievement, or a formal statement of an achievement.

core.definition: A reference that names the source of a quotation, idea, or fact, especially in academic or professional writing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'tay', the second syllable, and the 'ci' is pronounced like 'sy'. Do not reduce the 'tay' vowel, and end with a plain 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In legal or policy contexts it may refer to an official summons or traffic ticket, which can carry a negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American academic life, a citation is any formal reference to a source in a paper, usually in APA, MLA, or Chicago style. In everyday speech, Americans use 'citation' most often for a traffic or parking ticket, as in 'I got a citation for speeding'. Be careful to say 'ticket' in casual conversation, since 'citation' sounds more official.

distinctions.note: A quotation is the exact words taken from a source, while a citation is the reference that credits the source, which may or may not include a quotation.
Reference is a broader term that can include a bibliography entry or a general mention, while citation refers to the specific in-text acknowledgment of a source.

examples.everyday: I got a parking citation downtown, even though I paid the meter.
examples.professional: Before we publish the report, please check that every figure has a proper citation to the source dataset.
examples.analytical: The author's citation of Aquinas is accurate, but it does not establish the broader claim about natural law.

nuance.analogy: A citation is like a return address on a letter: it tells the reader exactly where the idea came from.
nuance.etymology: From Latin citatio, a summoning, from citare, to summon or set in motion.
common_mistakes: Using 'citation' as a verb, as in 'I citation the source'; the verb is 'cite'.
Confusing it with 'site' because the words sound alike when spoken quickly.

citation.etymology: From Middle English *citacioun*, from Old French *citation*, from Latin *citatio*.

senses.definition: A group of people hired to attend a performance and to either applaud or boo.
A group of fawning admirers.
A group of people who pre-arrange among themselves to express strong support for an idea, so as to give the false impression of a wider consensus.

core.definition: A group of people paid or organized to applaud, boo, or praise someone, creating a false impression of popular support.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short a as in cat and a hard k at the end. The French origin does not change the American pronunciation, so do not add a French nasal or an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that the support is staged, paid, or manipulative rather than genuine.
nuance.usage_note: Claque is mainly used in writing about theater, politics, media, and reviews. Americans rarely use it in casual speech, where they would say a planted crowd or paid fans. Use it when you want to suggest that applause or praise was arranged in advance.

distinctions.note: A fan base is made of genuine supporters, while a claque is organized to look like support whether or not people actually agree.
An entourage follows a celebrity for social or practical reasons, while a claque is specifically there to applaud or boo on cue.

collocations: to pack the room with a claque

examples.everyday: The guy in the front row is clearly part of a claque, because he starts clapping every time the singer hits a high note.
examples.professional: Our product launch felt staged, as if the vendor had brought in a claque to cheer every demo.
examples.analytical: The praise for the novel was partly the work of a claque hired by the publisher, which distorted the critical reception.

nuance.analogy: A claque is like a laugh track on a sitcom, supplying applause on cue so the room seems more enthusiastic than it really is.
nuance.etymology: From French claque, a slap or clap, from claquer, to clap; the word is imitative in origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as clake or with a long a.
Using claque for any group of fans, when it specifically implies paid or staged enthusiasm.

senses.definition: In a commensurate manner; so as to be equal or proportionate.
With equal measure or extent.

core.definition: In a way that matches in size, degree, or amount; in proportion to something else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on MEN. The -ately ending is weak: the middle syllables are reduced to a quick 'ur-ut' and the last syllable is 'lee.' Learners often stress the -ate syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and formal, so it works well in careful writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say this in casual conversation. It appears in reports, contracts, and policy writing, such as 'rewarded commensurately.' In speech, 'proportionally' or 'to match' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Proportionally is common in everyday and technical speech. Commensurately is more formal and emphasizes matching a measure.
Equally means the same amount for everyone. Commensurately means the amount changes to match something else.

examples.everyday: If your hours go up, your pay should go up commensurately, right?
examples.professional: Budget and headcount will be adjusted commensurately once the new scope is approved.
examples.analytical: Her moral claim grows commensurately with the harm she has suffered and the duty owed to her.

nuance.analogy: Like adding water to a recipe in the same ratio as the flour: when one changes, the other changes to keep the balance.
nuance.etymology: From commensurate plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -ate syllable: 'kuh-men-suh-RATE-lee.'
Using it in casual speech where 'proportionally' would sound more natural.
Confusing it with 'commiserately,' which is a different word.

senses.definition: The act of commiserating; sorrow for the hardships or afflictions of another; pity; compassion.

core.definition: Sympathy or shared sadness for someone's troubles, often expressed by sharing a similar experience or offering comfort.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on RAY, the '-ation' syllable, and the first syllable is weak. Learners often stress MIZ, which is wrong for this noun. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes warm, shared sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use commiseration in written or formal speech, such as a note, speech, or thoughtful message. In casual talk, people more often say 'I feel for you' or 'That sucks.' A natural reply to a friend's sympathy is 'Thanks for listening.'

distinctions.note: Sympathy is the general feeling of care for another's pain. Commiseration suggests sharing the sorrow or complaining together.
Compassion is an active care that wants to relieve suffering. Commiseration is a shared feeling of sadness.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the commiseration. I needed to vent about my landlord after that terrible day.
examples.professional: Her message to the affected engineers offered commiseration but gave no clear next steps.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophers debate whether mere commiseration differs from genuine concern for another's welfare.

nuance.analogy: Like sitting on the same porch step after a storm, sharing the sadness without fixing anything.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin commiseratio 'pity,' from commiserari 'to pity.'
common_mistakes: Stressing MIZ instead of RAY, as in 'KUH-miz-uh-ray-shun.'
Using 'commiseration' as a verb; the verb is 'commiserate.'
Confusing it with 'commiseration' sounds like 'commission' or 'commissary' in speech.

senses.definition: In AI: The text a language model generates to continue a prompt.
The act or state of being or making something complete; conclusion, accomplishment.
senses.example: The fundraising campaign was successfully stewarded to completion on time.

senses.definition: The conclusion of an act of conveyancing concerning the sale of a property.
A forward pass that is successfully caught by the intended receiver.
The act of making a metric space complete by adding points.
The space resulting from such an act.
Synonym of autocomplete.
senses.example: tab completion

senses.definition: Orgasm.

core.definition: The act of finishing something; in AI, the text a language model generates to continue a given prompt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLEE, the second syllable, and the -tion ending is a quick 'shun' with a reduced vowel. Don't stress the first syllable; say kum-PLEE-shun, not KOM-plee-shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday use it means finishing something; in AI it is a technical term with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English people usually say finish, done, or 'when it's done' rather than completion, which sounds formal or official, as in paperwork, a project milestone, or a course. In AI, a completion is the model's generated continuation of a prompt, and the term is common in API documentation, where a completion request returns text. Engineers say things like 'the completion came back empty' in chat. Use the technical sense only with people who work with models.

distinctions.note: Finish is the everyday verb and noun for ending something; completion is more formal and emphasizes the state of being done.
A conclusion is the end of an argument, event, or document; completion is the act of making something whole and finished.

examples.everyday: I'm waiting for the completion of the bathroom remodel, so the house is a mess right now.
examples.professional: The completion rate for the onboarding survey went up after we shortened it to five questions.
examples.analytical: A model's completion is only a probable continuation, so its fluency should not be taken as proof of understanding.

nuance.analogy: Like an improv partner who finishes your sentence with the most likely next words.
nuance.etymology: From Latin completio, from complere, to fill up or finish.
common_mistakes: Using completion for everyday 'finish' in casual speech, which sounds stiff; say 'when we finish' instead.
Stressing the first syllable: say kum-PLEE-shun, not KOM-plee-shun.
Confusing the noun with the verb: say 'the completion of the form', not 'I completion the form'.

conversation.text: The completion stopped mid-sentence because it hit the max tokens limit.
Older completion endpoints took raw text, while chat endpoints take a list of messages.
Project completion is scheduled for the end of the quarter.

senses.definition: The act or process of computing; calculation; reckoning.
The result of computation; the amount computed.

core.definition: The process of calculating a result, often through a sequence of mathematical or logical steps carried out by a computer.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TAY, and the 'pyoo' syllable is reduced to 'pyuh'. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, objective word with no emotional charge, though it can sound heavy in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use computation in science, engineering and computing contexts, and it often suggests a multistep process rather than a quick sum. In casual speech people say 'math' or 'the calculation'. In a work meeting, saying 'the computation takes about an hour' is natural, and a common reply is 'Can we speed it up?'

distinctions.note: Calculation is the general word for working out a number, while computation often implies a longer, systematic or automated process.
Computing is the broader field or activity of using computers, while computation is a specific calculation or the act of performing one.

examples.everyday: My phone takes a while to finish the computation when I run that photo filter.
examples.professional: The nightly model refresh is slow because the feature computation runs on a single machine.
examples.analytical: Every physical process can be described as a computation, but whether the universe itself computes is a contested question.

nuance.analogy: Think of computation as a long kitchen recipe that a machine follows step by step, while calculation is one quick mental sum.
nuance.etymology: From Latin computatio, 'a reckoning together', from computare.
common_mistakes: Using computation for a simple everyday sum, where calculation is more natural.
Confusing computation with computing, which refers to the field or activity in general.

computation.etymology: From late Middle English *computacioun*, from Middle French *computation*, from Latin *computatiō*, from *computare* (“sum up, reckon, compute”); see compute.

senses.definition: To end; to come to an end.
senses.example: The story concluded with a moral.

senses.definition: To bring to an end; to close; to finish.
To bring about as a result; to effect; to make.
senses.example: to conclude a bargain

senses.definition: To come to a conclusion, to a final decision.
senses.example: From the evidence, I conclude that this man was murdered.

senses.definition: To shut off; to restrain; to limit; to estop; to bar.
senses.example: The defendant is concluded by his own plea.

senses.definition: To deduce, to infer (develop a causal relation)

core.definition: To end something, or to reach a decision or judgment after considering evidence, facts or discussion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, klood, and the first syllable is very short and reduced to kun. The final d is a clear voiced sound, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal and deliberate than finish or end.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conclude in both speech and writing, though in casual talk they more often say wrap up or finish. In meetings, 'Let's conclude' signals the end of the agenda, and in writing 'I conclude that' is common. A natural reply to 'So what do you conclude?' is a brief summary such as 'I think the data points to a small but real effect.'

distinctions.note: Finish is everyday and general, while conclude suggests an orderly, formal or planned ending.
Decide means choosing an option, while conclude means reaching a judgment after reasoning about evidence.

examples.everyday: The movie concluded with a huge car chase, which I did not love.
examples.professional: Let's conclude the meeting by assigning an owner to each action item.
examples.analytical: From these results we can conclude that the effect is real but small, though the sample is limited.

nuance.analogy: Like closing a file folder after the last page has been signed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concludere, meaning to shut up or enclose, from con- 'together' and claudere 'to close'.
common_mistakes: Using conclude for a physical ending, as in 'the store concluded at nine'; say closed or ended instead.
Using conclude to with a noun or infinitive; use conclude that or conclude from.

conclude.etymology: From Middle English *concluden*, borrowed from Latin *conclūdō* (“to shut up, close, end”).

senses.definition: To puzzle, perplex, baffle, bewilder (somebody).
To mix up, muddle up (one thing with another); to mistake (one thing for another).
To mix thoroughly; to confound; to disorder.
To make uneasy and ashamed; to embarrass.
To rout; discomfit.
To be confused.
(of a person) unable to think clearly or understand.
(of a person or animal) disoriented.
Chaotic, jumbled or muddled.
Making no sense; illogical.
Embarrassed.

core.definition: Unable to think clearly or understand something; not sure what is happening, what to think, or what to do.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FYOOZD, and pronounce the final -ed as a /d/ sound because it follows a voiced z sound. Many learners add an extra syllable or say 'kon-FYOOST', which sounds wrong.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It describes a state of mind, and saying 'I'm confused' is an everyday, polite way to ask for clarification.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm confused' or 'I'm a little confused' in meetings and conversation to ask for explanation without sounding rude. It is more natural than 'I don't understand' in some settings because it sounds less like blaming the speaker. For a more sympathetic tone, say 'I'm a bit confused about...'.

distinctions.note: 'Confused' describes a person's state of mind, while 'confusing' describes the thing that causes confusion, such as 'a confusing instruction'.
'Puzzled' is milder and suggests a short moment of not understanding, while 'confused' often lasts longer or involves more disorientation.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm a little confused, did you say the meeting is at two or at three?
examples.professional: I'm confused about the ownership of this dashboard, so can we clarify who maintains it before we merge?
examples.analytical: A confused reader may be distinguished from a confident one, because the first lacks the conceptual frame needed to assign meaning to the argument.

nuance.analogy: Being confused is like walking into a dark room with no light: you know something is there, but you cannot see where things are or how to move.
nuance.etymology: From confuse, from Latin confusus, past participle of confundere, 'to pour together, mix up'.
common_mistakes: Using 'confusing' when describing a person, as in 'I am confusing', which means the thing is confusing rather than that you feel confused.
Pronouncing the final -ed as 't', as in 'kon-FYOOST'.
Confusing 'confused' with 'confusing' in written reports.

confused.etymology: Originally from Middle English *confused* (“frustrated, ruined”), from Anglo-Norman *confus* + Middle English *-ed*, from Latin *cōnfūsus*, past participle of *cōnfundō*; now equivalent to *confuse* *ed*.

conversation.text: I'm confused. Are we meeting at six or seven?
The directions were so confusing that we all got confused.
Sorry, you lost me. I'm a little confused.

senses.definition: Clipping of congratulations.
senses.example: You were cast in the show? Congrats!

senses.definition: Clipping of congratulations.
senses.example: Accept our congrats for all your hard work!

core.definition: A casual short way to say congratulations when someone has good news or has achieved something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, GRATS, and the first vowel is a reduced uh sound. Do not say KON-grats with a strong o.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It is warm but casual, so it fits friends and coworkers better than formal situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Congrats!' casually to friends, coworkers, or on social media after a promotion, engagement, or new baby. Avoid it in formal letters or with someone you do not know well; use 'Congratulations' instead. A natural reply is 'Thanks!' or 'Thank you, I'm so excited.'

distinctions.note: Congratulations is the full, polite form for any situation. Congrats is casual and friendly.
Well done praises a specific effort or result. Congrats celebrates an event, such as a wedding or a job offer.

examples.everyday: Congrats on the new house! When do you move in?
examples.professional: Congrats on shipping the Q3 release, the whole team worked really hard on it.
examples.analytical: A quick congrats in a department email is ritual, but it still signals warmth and recognition of the work.

nuance.analogy: Like a quick high five in words: warm, short, and casual.
nuance.etymology: Clipping of congratulations, from Latin congratulari, 'to rejoice with'.
common_mistakes: Using congrats in formal writing or to a senior person you do not know well.
Saying kon-GRATS with a long o instead of the reduced uh sound in the first syllable.

conversation.text: Congrats on the new job! When do you start?
I heard you got engaged. Congrats!
"We bought a house!" "Congrats, you guys! That's so exciting."

senses.definition: Either term of a conjunction.
An adjunct that supplements a sentence with information, connecting the sentence with previous parts of the discourse. Not considered to be an essential part of the propositional content.
(rare) Either term of a conjunctive conjunction.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Conjoined.
senses.example: Set A is conjunct with set B.

senses.definition: Acting together; collaborative.

core.definition: In logic, either of the statements joined by 'and' in a conjunction, such as p and q in 'p ∧ q'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a short 'uh' vowel in the second syllable. As an adjective meaning 'joined together', the stress often moves to the second syllable: kun-JUNKT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in logic and grammar.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'conjunct' almost only in logic, philosophy, and computer science. In everyday speech, people say 'part' or 'condition', as in 'both conditions must be met'. You may also see it in linguistics, where it means a sentence adjunct joined to other material.

distinctions.note: 'Conjunction' is the whole combined statement or the connecting word. 'Conjunct' is one of the parts being joined.
A disjunct is joined by 'or' in logic. A conjunct is joined by 'and'.

examples.everyday: If someone says 'I want pizza and I want it cheap,' each half is a conjunct of that wish.
examples.professional: The filter requires both conjuncts to be true, so we should check the age and region conditions separately.
examples.analytical: In 'p and q,' the whole is true only if each conjunct is true, which is why Boolean filters split into independent conditions.

nuance.analogy: It's like a two-key safe: each conjunct is a key, and both must turn before the door opens.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conjunctus, the past participle of conjungere, 'to join together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'conjunct' with 'conjunction', which refers to the operation or the connecting word.
Using 'conjunct' in everyday speech, where 'part' or 'condition' sounds more natural.

conjunct.etymology: From Latin *conjunctus*, the perfect past participle of *conjungō*.

senses.definition: An agreement on some data value that is needed during computation.
A process of decision-making that seeks widespread agreement among group members.
General agreement among the members of a given group or community, each member of which exercises some discretion in decision-making and follow-up action.
senses.example: reach consensus

senses.definition: Average projected value.
senses.example: a financial consensus forecast

senses.definition: To seek consensus; to hold discussions with the aim of reaching mutual agreement.

core.definition: A general agreement among the members of a group, reached after discussion and with the support of most or all of them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SEN, the second syllable. The first syllable is a reduced kuhn, and the final -sus is a soft uhs, not a long ee or oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fairness, shared understanding, and cooperation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use consensus often in workplace meetings, politics, and news, such as 'we reached a consensus' or 'there is a broad consensus that...' In casual talk people say 'everyone agreed' or 'we're all on the same page.' Avoid saying 'consensus' when only two people agree; it suggests a group decision.

distinctions.note: Agreement can be between two people or a group. Consensus specifically refers to a broad group opinion reached through discussion.
A majority is a larger number of votes for one option. Consensus means most people accept the outcome, even if some still disagree.

examples.everyday: Our neighbors finally reached a consensus about where to put the new playground.
examples.professional: Let's get consensus on the API design before we start writing the tickets.
examples.analytical: Habermas treats consensus not as a given but as the outcome of rational public discourse among free participants.

nuance.analogy: Consensus is like a group of friends agreeing on a restaurant after everyone has said what they want: no one is fully happy, but everyone can live with it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consensus 'agreement, harmony,' from consentire 'to feel together, agree.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'a consensus with him' when one person agrees; in American usage it usually refers to a group, so say 'agreement with him.'
Using 'consensus' as a verb in formal writing; say 'reach consensus' or 'build consensus' instead, although it is used informally.

consensus.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *cōnsēnsus* (“agreement, accordance, unanimity”), from *cōnsentiō* (“feel together; agree”); see *consent*.

conversation.text: We didn't reach a consensus, so we'll vote next week.
The consensus is that we should launch in the fall.
Let's try to build consensus before we present this to leadership.

senses.definition: Relating to or causing construction.
Carefully considered and meant to be helpful.
Serving a useful purpose.
Deemed after the fact to exist or to have occurred, despite the formal process not having been followed; often when there was no intention to do so at the time.
senses.example: constructive dismissal

senses.definition: Not direct or expressed, but inferred.

core.definition: Meant to help improve something; useful and positive, as in feedback, criticism, or suggestions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, STRUK. The vowel in the first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final -tive is 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. Calling feedback constructive signals that it is intended to help, not to attack.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'constructive feedback' or 'constructive criticism' in workplaces, schools, and meetings to soften a critique. It is polite and professional. Saying 'That wasn't very constructive' can sound like a sharp complaint that the idea was unhelpful.

distinctions.note: 'Critical' can mean harshly negative, while 'constructive' means negative points offered in order to help.
'Helpful' is general and casual; 'constructive' implies careful thought and an aim to improve a plan or work.

examples.everyday: Your advice about the recipe was constructive, so I'll try a little less salt next time.
examples.professional: Thanks for the constructive comments on the draft; I've revised the section on sampling bias.
examples.analytical: Constructive criticism presupposes a shared goal, without which critique becomes mere opposition.

nuance.analogy: Constructive feedback is like a good map: it points out the road you missed and helps you get there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin constructivus, from construere, 'to build, pile together'.
common_mistakes: Using 'constructive' to mean 'constructed' or 'built'; in a general sense, 'constructive' means helpful.
Confusing it with 'destructive', its opposite.

senses.definition: A woman who flirts or plays with people's affections.
Any hummingbird in the genus Lophornis.
Of or relating to a feminine style of clothing involving ribbons, frills, and bows.

core.definition: A woman who flirts with people, playing with their affections without serious intent.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final t is a crisp, unaspirated stop. Do not say the final syllable as 'ket' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly disapproving. It suggests a woman who uses charm to attract admiration, often without sincerity, and it can sound old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, literature, or commentary about a person's flirtatious behavior. In casual speech they usually say flirt or tease. Calling someone a coquette is a judgment, so it can offend.

distinctions.note: A flirt is the everyday, neutral word for someone playing with attraction; coquette is more literary and carries a sense of calculated, self-centered teasing.
Tease describes playful provoking in general, while coquette specifically describes a woman's cultivated charm for attracting admirers.

examples.everyday: My sister says her new coworker is a bit of a coquette, but I think he is just friendly.
examples.professional: In the meeting notes, the reviewer described the marketing pitch as coquettish, meaning it teased the client without making any real commitment.
examples.analytical: Austen's heroines often resist the coquette's manipulation, since the coquette treats affection as a game rather than a moral commitment.

nuance.analogy: A coquette is like a lamp that draws moths: bright and inviting, but the light is meant to attract attention rather than to warm anyone.
nuance.etymology: From French coquette, the feminine of coquet, meaning flirtatious, from coq, rooster.
common_mistakes: Using coquette as a general adjective for any flirtatious act; the adjective is coquettish.
Confusing the noun with the hummingbird sense, which is rare in everyday American talk.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: Any of many species of marine invertebrates in the class Anthozoa, most of which build hard calcium carbonate skeletons and form colonies, or a colony belonging to one of those species.
A hard substance made of the skeletons of these organisms.
A somewhat yellowish orange-pink color; the color of red coral (Corallium rubrum) of the Mediterranean Sea, commonly used as an ornament or gem.
senses.example: coral:

senses.definition: The ovaries of a cooked lobster; so called from their color.
(historical) A piece of coral, usually fitted with small bells and other appurtenances, used by children as a plaything.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Made of coral.
Having the orange-pink color of coral.

core.definition: A hard, colorful skeleton formed by tiny sea animals, or the animals that build it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the second syllable as a reduced schwa with a light l. Do not pronounce it as two full syllables, 'kor-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It can also suggest beauty, warmth, or tropical settings in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coral in everyday talk for the color, for ocean reefs, and for jewelry. The color sense is very common in clothing and paint descriptions. In technical biology the animal sense is also used, especially in marine science.

distinctions.note: A coral reef is a structure built by coral colonies; coral alone can refer to the animal, skeleton, or color.
Salmon is a fish color that can look similar; coral is a more pinkish or orange-pink shade often used for paint and fashion.

examples.everyday: We went snorkeling last summer and saw bright fish swimming around the coral.
examples.professional: The design team picked a coral accent color for the app's buttons because it felt warm and friendly.
examples.analytical: Coral is a living organism and a mineral-like structure, which makes it a useful example of how biological processes produce geological features.

nuance.analogy: Coral is like a city built one brick at a time by tiny workers, with each new layer resting on the skeletons of the last.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corallium, from Greek korallion, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with two full syllables, 'kor-al'.
Confusing coral the color with the color of the Mediterranean red coral sense.
Using coral as a verb in everyday English, which is not standard.
nuance.biblical_note: In Job 28:18 coral is mentioned as a precious item that cannot compare with wisdom. The Hebrew word here is ra'moth, usually rendered as coral in translations, and the verse uses it to say that wisdom is worth more than valuable materials.

coral.etymology: From Old French *coral*, from Latin *corallium*, from Ancient Greek *κοράλλιον* (“coral”).

senses.definition: Asking someone to speak up because you can't hear well.

core.definition: A polite request asking someone to talk at a higher volume because you cannot hear them well.

pronunciation.respelling: kood yoo speek uh LIT-uhl LOW-der
pronunciation.tip: Little has its primary stress on the first syllable (LIT-tl), and louder ends in an r-colored schwa (LOW-der). The a in a is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it is a helpful request that people accept without offense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this on the phone, in noisy restaurants, or when someone speaks softly in a meeting. It is courteous, and you can soften it further with 'Sorry, could you speak a little louder?' A typical reply is 'Oh, sure, is this better?'

distinctions.vs: speak a little louder vs. speak up
distinctions.note: Speak up is shorter and more casual; speak a little louder is more polite and specific.
Louder is the standard comparative of loud; more loudly is grammatically possible but less natural.

examples.everyday: The TV is really loud in here. Could you speak a little louder?
examples.professional: Could you speak a little louder? The people on the video call can't hear the back of the room.
examples.analytical: Could you speak a little louder? I want to hear the full reasoning of the argument before I respond.

nuance.analogy: Like turning up the volume on a radio that is playing too softly for the room.
nuance.etymology: Speak comes from Old English specan; louder comes from Old English hlūd, loud, with the comparative suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Speak more louder' with a double comparative.
Pronouncing louder with a clear second syllable (LOW-der) instead of a reduced r-colored ending.

conversation.text: Could you speak a little louder? I'm on a busy street.
"Could you speak a little louder?" "Sure. Is this better?"

senses.definition: Any bird of the family Gruidae, large birds with long legs and a long neck which is extended during flight.
Ardea herodias, the great blue heron.
A mechanical lifting machine or device, often used for lifting heavy loads for industrial or construction purposes.
An iron arm with horizontal motion, attached to the side or back of a fireplace for supporting kettles etc. over the fire.
A siphon, or bent pipe, for drawing liquors out of a cask.
A forked post or projecting bracket to support spars, etc. generally used in pairs.
To extend (one's neck).
To raise or lower with, or as if with, a crane.
To pull up before a jump.

core.definition: A tall, long-legged bird with a long neck, or a large machine with a long arm used to lift heavy loads at construction sites.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and make the diphthong glide smoothly from 'ay' to 'n'. Be sure to pronounce the r clearly at the start, since American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The bird sense is descriptive, and the machine sense is practical and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use crane for the construction machine, especially when they see a tower crane over a building site. The bird sense appears in nature writing and in Bible translations. The verb 'to crane your neck' is a common everyday expression meaning to stretch your neck to see something.

distinctions.note: A heron is a long-legged wading bird, often with a short neck pulled into an S-shape in flight; a crane has a longer, straighter neck that extends forward in flight.
A hoist is any device for lifting, often a simple winch; a crane is a larger machine with a movable arm or boom.

examples.everyday: Everyone on the sidewalk was craning their necks to see the parade float.
examples.professional: The site manager said the tower crane will be moved before the steel delivery arrives on Monday.
examples.analytical: In Isaiah the crane is used as an image of mourning, a bird whose cry expresses grief and lament.

nuance.analogy: A construction crane is like a giant arm with a hand at the end, lifting weight that a human arm could never move.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cran, the bird, related to Greek geranos, crane; the machine sense developed later from the bird's long neck and arm-like shape.
common_mistakes: Confusing crane (bird or machine) with crank, which is a handle or a grouchy person.
Saying 'crane my neck' without a clear object; the usual phrase is 'crane your neck to see something'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV the crane is named among birds that keep the time of their migration, and in Isaiah it is compared to a bird whose cry is mourning. The Hebrew word translated crane is debated among scholars, so translations vary. Isaiah 38:14 describes the sick king Hezekiah's lament, comparing his cry to a swallow or a crane. Jeremiah 8:7 contrasts the migrating birds' sense of seasons with Israel's failure to know the Lord's judgment.

crane.etymology: From Middle English *crane*, from Old English *cran* (“crane”), from **kran*, **kranō*, from Proto-Germanic **kranô* (“crane”), from Proto-Indo-European **gerh₂-* (“to cry hoarsely”).

senses.definition: A sideboard or buffet.
A horizontal filing cabinet, typically placed behind a desk.

core.definition: A long, low piece of furniture with cabinets or drawers, used as a sideboard in a dining room or as a storage cabinet behind a desk.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -DEN-, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. Don't say the final a as 'ah'; it is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes furniture and carries a faint hint of mid-century or upscale home decor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use credenza mostly for a low, long cabinet in a dining room or living room, or for a low storage piece behind an executive desk in an office. In everyday talk many people would just say sideboard or buffet for the first sense. Saying credenza in a furniture store or with a designer is natural.

distinctions.note: A sideboard is the general term for a dining-room cabinet; credenza is the same kind of piece, often sleeker or more modern in style.
In American usage buffet usually refers to a dining-room server or the meal itself, so it can be confused with the furniture sense.
A credenza sits behind a desk as a storage surface, while the desk is the main work surface.

examples.everyday: We put the wedding photos on the credenza in the dining room.
examples.professional: Can you move the printer off the credenza so we have room for the conference phone?
examples.analytical: The mid-century credenza signals a shift toward furniture that is both functional and visually restrained.

nuance.analogy: A credenza is like a low shelf with doors that sits behind a desk and holds everything you need within reach.
nuance.etymology: From Italian credenza, meaning a sideboard, from credere, to believe, from the idea of a trusted place for things.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KRED-en-za) instead of the second.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'den-ZAH' with a strong final ah.

senses.definition: To get to the point; to get on with it; to state something directly.
senses.example: We don't have much time here. Could you cut to the chase?

core.definition: To stop talking around a subject and get directly to the point, saying what matters most.

pronunciation.tip: 'Chase' is the main stress, so say 'kut-too-thuh-CHAYS'. 'To' is reduced to 'tu' or 'tuh', and 'the' is reduced to 'thuh' before the consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, but can sound impatient if said to someone who is trying to explain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in meetings, at work, and with friends when someone is being too long-winded. It is often said politely, such as 'Can we cut to the chase?' It can be blunt, so use it with care with people who are not your close friends. A natural reply is 'Sure, the bottom line is we're over budget.'

distinctions.note: 'Get to the point' is more neutral and polite, while 'cut to the chase' is more informal and can sound impatient.
'Bottom line' is a noun phrase for the final result or conclusion, while 'cut to the chase' describes the action of getting there.

collocations: cut to the chase in the meeting
cut to the chase and tell me
cut to the chase on the numbers

examples.everyday: Okay, I'm running late, so can you cut to the chase and tell me where the keys are?
examples.professional: Thanks for the background, but can we cut to the chase and go over the revenue impact?
examples.analytical: A good argument does not merely pile up details; it cuts to the chase and shows why the claim matters.

nuance.analogy: Like skipping the opening credits of a movie and going straight to the main scene.
nuance.etymology: Originally American slang from the 1900s, from 'cut' (to take a shortcut) and 'chase' (the hunt or pursuit).
common_mistakes: Saying 'cut to a chase' with an article, instead of 'cut to the chase'.
Using it as a noun phrase, when it is a verb phrase in the imperative or infinitive.

cut-to-the-chase.etymology: From cinema usage: to cut so as to get to the exciting part.

conversation.text: Let's cut to the chase: can we afford this or not?
I'll cut to the chase. We need two more engineers.
He talked for twenty minutes before finally cutting to the chase.

core.definition: An island country in the eastern Mediterranean Sea, south of Turkey. In the Bible it is the island where Barnabas came from and where the early church first spread.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is reduced, so it sounds like 'SY-pruhs.' Do not pronounce the 'u' as 'oo' or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a place and carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Cyprus for the country and the island, and they often mention it in travel, news and Mediterranean geography. The name is also used for the divided island, with the Republic of Cyprus recognized internationally. Be careful not to confuse it with the tree cypress, which sounds identical.

distinctions.note: Cypress is the evergreen tree; Cyprus is the island, and they are pronounced identically but have different meanings.

examples.everyday: We spent our vacation in Cyprus, swimming in the warm sea and eating fresh seafood.
examples.professional: Our European office has a team based in Cyprus, so the calls are scheduled around the Eastern time zone difference.
examples.analytical: Acts records that the early church spread to Cyprus, and Barnabas, himself from there, became a central missionary figure.

nuance.analogy: Cyprus is like a stepping stone between three continents, sitting in the sea where Europe, Asia and Africa meet.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Kypros, a name whose origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing the island with the tree cypress, which sounds the same.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the final 'us' as 'oos'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek the island is Kypros. Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). Believers from Cyprus helped spread the gospel to Antioch (Acts 11:19-20). Paul and Barnabas later preached on the island, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus became a believer (Acts 13:4-12). Paul's ship also sailed past Cyprus on his voyage to Rome (Acts 27:4).

senses.definition: A road-to-Damascus moment: a sudden, complete change of mind or belief.

core.definition: The ancient capital city of Syria, a major city in the Bible where Saul of Tarsus had his conversion on the road to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MAS. The final -us is a weak, reduced vowel, and the ending is not pronounced like 'Damask-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a place name with strong historical and religious associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say Damascus in both news and church settings, and it is pronounced consistently. In Bible study it is often mentioned in connection with the conversion of Paul, so a natural conversation might start with 'Have you read about the road to Damascus?' Note that the phrase 'road to Damascus' describes a sudden conversion.

distinctions.note: Damask is a patterned fabric that is named after Damascus, where it was historically made; the place and the fabric are different words.

examples.everyday: We drove through the old streets of Damascus when we visited Syria years ago.
examples.professional: Our travel group book included a stop in Damascus as part of the historical tour.
examples.analytical: Acts presents the conversion near Damascus as a decisive turning point in the spread of the gospel.

nuance.analogy: Like a crossroads on a map where a traveler's life suddenly changes direction.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew 'Dammeseq,' the Hebrew name of the city, from Aramaic and Semitic roots.
common_mistakes: Saying 'duh-MASK-us' with a hard 'k' in the final syllable.
Confusing the city with the fabric 'damask'.
nuance.biblical_note: Damascus appears in the Old Testament as the capital of Aram (Syria), and in the New Testament as the city where Saul was struck down on the road and converted (Acts 9:1-19). Abraham's servant Eliezer is associated with the city in Genesis 15:2. The city is also mentioned in Isaiah 7:8 as a center of Aramean power.

senses.definition: Any of the genus Lolium of grasses, especially as a weed in wheat fields.
Especially, the species Lolium temulentum, often host to a fungus toxic to humans and animals.

core.definition: A grass of the genus Lolium that grows as a weed among wheat; the species Lolium temulentum is often infected with a toxic fungus.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r is strongly pronounced in General American. The final syllable is a reduced vowel, so say it as 'nuhl', not 'nell'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a botanical or biblical term with no emotional charge outside its agricultural or scriptural context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word outside botany, agriculture, or Bible study. In a Bible study or sermon you might hear it as a weed resembling wheat. Most people would just say weed or ryegrass in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Ryegrass is a cultivated forage grass in the same genus; darnel is the weedy, often toxic relative that infests grain fields.
Tares is the RSV term in Matthew 13 for the same weed; darnel is the modern botanical name.

examples.everyday: My grandmother pointed out that the weed in her wheat field was darnel, and she pulled it out by hand.
examples.professional: The agronomy report flagged darnel infestation in the northern plots, which can reduce grain quality.
examples.analytical: The parable's imagery of darnel among the wheat raises questions about the coexistence of good and evil in the present age.
